proposals.name: Strategy stated first, key object derived not asserted
proposals.instruction: Score how much the post (a) announces the governing plan before executing it, and (b) shows where its central construction/substitution/auxiliary object came from. 10 = the post opens by saying what will be reduced to what ('it suffices to find three numbers whose pairwise sums are squares, then pigeonhole'), and then produces the needed object by solving for it (setting up the three equations and subtracting to isolate x, y, z). 0 = the central object appears out of nowhere as a bare 'Let a = 2x^2-4x, b = 2x^2+1, c = 2x^2+4x' or 'consider the triple ...' with no plan announced and no indication of how it was found, even if everything afterwards is airtight. Score 5 if the plan is stated but the object is still asserted, or vice versa.
proposals.rationale: R35, R20 and R55 all use literally the same triple on the same problem, yet R35 (dense 0.889) narrates the pigeonhole plan, derives the triple by solving three simultaneous square conditions, and then bounds it, while R20 (dense 0.351, card 0.927) and R55 (dense 0.375, card 0.935) assert the triple and verify. The scorecard is nearly indifferent among the three; the derivation/assertion split is the one visible thing that separates them. R38 likewise asserts its x^2,y^2,z^2 selection with 'I claim that we can select'.

proposals.name: Post self-brands its route as a deviation or a stunt
proposals.instruction: Read only the post's own self-description of its method. 10 = the post presents its argument as the plain way to do the problem, with no disclaimer. 0 = the post explicitly labels its own route as off the beaten path or as a joke: 'Scuffed troll solution', 'Oversimplified solution', 'ridiculous and yet ultimately equivalent overkill', 'A different solution for those who understand less about ...', 'my solution during the contest (different from the others)', 'Instead of the usual three number construction, I used seven numbers', 'fakesolve', 'very cheap but fast solution', 'Here is my cursed solution'. Intermediate scores for milder hedges ('Does this work?', 'similar to above'). Judge the self-labeling only; do not judge whether the mathematics is good.
proposals.rationale: R48 (dense 0.105, card 0.760) says in so many words that it replaced the usual three-number construction with a seven-number odd cycle, and is the lowest dense rank in the slice; R44 (dense 0.140, card 0.848) advertises itself as finite-field overkill; R23 (dense 0.274, card 0.923) calls itself a troll solution; R21, R52, R46 and R11 carry the same kind of self-label and all sit dense-low / card-high. The scorecard scores the executed mathematics and ignores the author's own framing of the route.

proposals.name: Names the pivotal idea in plain words
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post explicitly identifies the one hinge on which the problem turns, in words a reader could repeat, independent of whether the post executes anything. 10 = the hinge is stated outright as a sentence or a displayed identity: 'F_{2n}/F_n = F_{n+1}+F_{n-1}', 'the problem is equivalent to minimizing AI_1 * AI_2, and AI_1*AI_2 = AX*AI so minimize AX', 'the monovariant is the difference between the largest and smallest a_i'. 0 = the post performs computation or case analysis from which a reader could not extract any statement of what the key idea was. Terseness must not be penalized and length must not be rewarded: a one-line post that states the hinge scores 10.
proposals.rationale: R03 (dense 0.817, card 0.121) is one identity plus self-deprecation; R13 (dense 0.778, card 0.108) is a three-line sketch that names the reduction; R43 (dense 0.684, card 0.053) and R22 (dense 0.638, card 0.045) contain no executed mathematics at all yet name the monovariant / the induction quantity in prose. All four are dense-high and card-bottom, so the scorecard appears to be measuring executed work and missing idea-naming.

proposals.name: Brevity concentrated on the hinge versus brevity by outsourcing
proposals.instruction: This applies to short posts (roughly under 10 lines of mathematics); score longer posts 5. Among short posts: 10 = the post is short because it states the structural fact that makes the problem collapse and nothing else (a closed form for F_{2n}/F_n; 'minimize AX since AI is fixed'; a power-of-a-point / triangle-inequality equality condition). 0 = the post is short because it hands the problem to a formula or a routine computation and reports the output, so that no structural fact about this problem is visible ('by the hook-length formula the answer is 9!/(...) = 42'; a two-line arithmetic of Pythagorean lengths).
proposals.rationale: R03 (0.817) and R13 (0.778) are both extremely short and dense-high; R29 (dense 0.254, card 0.953) and R47 (dense 0.330, card 0.929) are equally short and dense-low. Raw length therefore cannot be what separates them, and the scorecard's treatment of the four is close to reversed; what differs is whether the short content is a structural fact about this configuration or a plugged-in formula.

proposals.name: Single external theorem does all the work
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the argument is discharged by invoking one heavy named or external result whose statement is not proved or unpacked in the post. 10 = no such invocation; every step is carried out on the objects of the problem. 0 = essentially the whole problem is dispatched by one citation - the hook-length formula for Young tableaux (with a link), Minkowski's inequality applied once to get the answer, a scaling trick that manufactures the answer in two lines - so that the post contains almost no reasoning specific to this problem. Mid scores when a named result is invoked but substantial problem-specific work surrounds it.
proposals.rationale: R29 (dense 0.254, card 0.953) is a single hook-length citation with an external URL; R32 (dense 0.268, card 0.901) is one application of Minkowski; R33 (dense 0.108, card 0.729) is a one-shot scaling construction. All three are near the top of the scorecard and near the bottom of the dense ranking, so a rubric that credits correctness and concision will over-reward exactly this shape.

proposals.name: Exploits the multiple-choice option list
proposals.instruction: For posts on problems that display answer choices (A)-(E). 10 = the post determines the answer as a value, never using the option list except to report the letter at the end. 0 = the option list is load-bearing: the post computes a residue or parity and picks the unique surviving choice, or argues that the choices are far enough apart that a coarse computation distinguishes them, or works in a substitute setting on the grounds that the listed answers are distinguishable there. Score 5 if the option list is used only as a final sanity check on an independently obtained value. Score 5 for problems with no answer choices.
proposals.rationale: R52 (dense 0.324, card 0.886) admits it is 'very cheap' and selects the only choice that is odd and 1 mod 3; R44 (dense 0.140, card 0.848) argues explicitly that 'the answer choices are all clearly distinct and extant over F_25' and then works there; R23 (dense 0.274, card 0.923) approximates its way to a neighbourhood of 72 and reads off a choice. All three are card-top and dense-low, so the scorecard is crediting a shortcut that does not answer the underlying question.

proposals.name: Load-bearing guess or approximation, patched afterwards
proposals.instruction: Score whether the decisive step is an unmotivated guess or a numerical approximation that the post then tries to justify. 10 = every decisive step is deduced; nothing is assumed and later checked. 0 = the post writes something like 'let a^2 = ab = b^2 since a and b differ by only 2, thus a^2 = 5184.3' and then locates the answer by proximity, or 'assume that the points form a right angle at (1,2)' and then verifies that assumption by substitution. Mid scores when a guess is made but the verification is complete and the guess is clearly signposted as a shortcut.
proposals.rationale: R23 (dense 0.274, card 0.923) sets three unequal quantities equal to each other to get a non-integer 5184.3 and then reasons by nearness to 72^2; R17 (dense 0.238, card 0.876) assumes the right angle and then confirms it with a perpendicular-line computation. Both read as rigorous to a criterion bank that checks 'are the steps justified', because the patching is present, yet both are dense-low.

proposals.name: Asserts a solution versus queries or corrects one
proposals.instruction: Score the speech act of the post. 10 = the post advances its own argument and stands behind it, ending in a stated answer or a QED. 0 = the post's actual purpose is to ask a question or to contest someone else - 'Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?', 'I am confused on the wiki solution #2 for this ... Wouldn't that be overcounting?', '@above that is listing everything out ... 7/20 is not .7' - even when a complete and well-written derivation is embedded inside the post. Score the framing, not the embedded mathematics.
proposals.rationale: R14 (dense 0.161, card 0.848) contains a fully worked and well-presented count and then asks why it is wrong; R30 (dense 0.206, card 0.769) reproduces a derivation only to challenge it; R01 (dense 0.432, card 0.995 - the single highest card rank in the slice) is a correction aimed at another poster with a one-line computation attached. A criterion bank scoring the embedded derivation will rank these at the very top.

proposals.name: Synthetic structural geometry versus coordinate or complex bash
proposals.instruction: For geometry problems only; score 5 for non-geometry posts. 10 = the argument proceeds through the configuration itself - angle chases, cyclic quadrilaterals, power of a point, identified centers, similar triangles - so that the geometric reason for the conclusion is visible. 0 = the configuration is replaced at the outset by coordinates, complex numbers on the unit circle, or trigonometric algebra, and the conclusion emerges from an algebraic identity being real or zero, with no geometric statement recovered. Intermediate when a synthetic reduction is finished by a short computation.
proposals.rationale: R11 (dense 0.056, the lowest in the slice, card 0.619) tosses an incenter configuration onto the complex plane and checks a ratio is real; R17 (dense 0.238, card 0.876) replaces an angle-between-lines question with explicit coordinates. Against these, R45 (0.833), R12 (0.792) and R41 (0.762) are all synthetic and dense-high. The scorecard scores the complex-number computation as clean and complete.

proposals.name: Identifies named configuration landmarks along the way
proposals.instruction: Score how many pivotal intermediate facts the post names as recognizable objects rather than deriving anonymously. 10 = the post says things like 'D is the circumcenter of ABC', 'by Radical Axes K lies on XY', 'by Miquel's theorem AKBX is cyclic', 'K is the midpoint of the A-symmedian chord', 'this is the equality case of Cauchy-Schwarz', so that the write-up is a chain of recognized landmarks. 0 = the post reaches the same place through unnamed algebra or unlabelled steps, with no intermediate object ever identified. This is about naming intermediate structure inside the argument, not about citing one external theorem that ends the problem (see A05).
proposals.rationale: R41 (dense 0.762, card 0.175) names radical axes, Miquel, the symmedian and the Dumpty point; R45 (dense 0.833, card 0.132) names the tangent intersection, the symmedian chord and offers inversion as an alternative; R12 (dense 0.792, card 0.198) identifies the circumcenter and finishes by radical axis; R19 (dense 0.865, card 0.217) names the Cauchy-Schwarz equality case. All four are card-low, so the bank appears not to credit landmark identification.

proposals.name: Executes the problem type's standard scaffolding step by step
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post sets up and works the routine machinery of its problem genre explicitly. For functional equations, 10 = 'let P(x,y) denote the assertion', followed by a visible ladder of specific substitutions (P(0,0), P(x,0), P(x,x^2), P(-x,0)) each with its consequence written out, building f(0)=0, evenness, and an identity for f(f(x)). For induction/recursion problems, 10 = the recursion is stated as a lemma, small values are tabulated, the pattern is conjectured and then proved. 0 = the post jumps between conclusions without exhibiting the substitutions or values that produced them, or replaces the genre machinery with an unrelated device.
proposals.rationale: R24 (0.994), R16 (0.972), R58 (0.972), R25 (0.965), R28/R56 (0.931 each) and R26 (0.921) are the highest dense ranks in the slice and every one of them lays out the substitution ladder or the tabulate-conjecture-induct ladder explicitly; their card ranks run only 0.067-0.387. R04 (dense 0.865, card 0.251) does the same with an explicit table of f(x) parities.

proposals.name: Names and closes the known failure mode of its own route
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post identifies the specific way its argument could fail and closes it. 10 = the post names the trap and disposes of it - 'to start fixing pointwise trap', 'we now deal with the pointwise trap' followed by the case split, 'we need not check for the pointwise trap because f(c)/c^2 is fixed and cannot alternate', or an explicit handling of small n / boundary values before the general argument. 0 = the post reaches a pointwise or generic conclusion and treats it as final without noticing that the conclusion was only established value-by-value or only for large parameters.
proposals.rationale: R18 (dense 0.931, card 0.310), R31 (dense 0.921, card 0.232) and R57 (dense 0.844, card 0.248) each name the pointwise trap in those words and dispatch it, and all three are dense-high with card ranks around 0.2-0.3. R07 (dense 0.142, card 0.793) is the mirror image: it argues the maximum is attained at the boundary and simply stops, without evaluating the boundary or addressing equality, yet the scorecard places it high.

proposals.name: Density of formal Claim / Lemma / Proof scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Purely a presentational measure. 10 = the post is organized into labelled Claims or Lemmas each with its own Proof and closing box, with aligned displayed equations and a final QED. 0 = no such apparatus at all: running prose, a bare identity, or an unlabelled paragraph. Do not judge correctness, difficulty, or approach - only how much formal proof-document furniture is present.
proposals.rationale: This isolates the presentational rigor that the scorecard appears to be rewarding on its own. R10 (dense 0.226, card 0.875) and R49 (dense 0.160, card 0.757) are the most heavily lemma-structured posts in the slice and are dense-low; R05 (dense 0.281, card 0.921) is a boxed Claim with an aligned chain of equivalences and is card-top. Against them, R03 (dense 0.817, card 0.121) and R13 (dense 0.778, card 0.108) have zero apparatus and are dense-high. Scored with the sign the fit chooses, this criterion should absorb the scorecard's polish bias.

proposals.name: Engages structure beyond the question asked
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post, after or while answering, states further structural facts about the same configuration - a generalization of the computation to arbitrary n, the limiting behaviour, additional derived relations, alternative routes to an intermediate step. 10 = the post supplies a substantive extension or a set of extra observations tied to this configuration. 0 = the post supplies exactly what was asked and stops. Do not reward off-topic chatter; the extension must be mathematical and about this problem's objects.
proposals.rationale: R36 (dense 0.889, card 0.123) answers the triangle random-walk question in one line and then develops the general n-gon distribution with roots of unity and its limit; R41 (dense 0.762, card 0.175) appends an 'Other Observations' block deriving CY/YD and the angle bisection. Both are dense-high and card-low, suggesting the bank treats the extra material as irrelevant or as dilution while the dense model reads it as engagement with the structure.

proposals.name: Mathematical substance relative to autobiographical narration
proposals.instruction: Score the fraction of the post that is mathematical content as opposed to narration about the solver's experience (how long it took, what they tried, regret, emotion, scores received, thanks to other posters). 10 = essentially all mathematical content. 0 = essentially all narration with no mathematical statement recoverable. Judge proportion only; do not penalize informal register, lowercase, slang or emoticons in the mathematical parts, and do not reward formal tone by itself.
proposals.rationale: This separates register from content, which the disagreement seems to hinge on. R03 (dense 0.817, card 0.121) is one correct identity buried in several lines of 'rip me fr'; R13 (dense 0.778, card 0.108) closes with 'surprisingly this was the first solution i thought of'; R22 (dense 0.638, card 0.045) and R53 (dense 0.643, card 0.033) are almost pure narration and receive the two lowest card ranks in the slice while sitting mid-to-high on dense. A bank that mixes register into its quality judgments will bottom out all four together.

proposals.name: Back-reference language presupposing earlier posts in the thread
proposals.instruction: Read only the problem and this one post. Score 0-10 how much of the post's language presupposes that other posts already exist in this thread and positions this post relative to them. Count: direct address to another poster ('@above', 'thanks!', 'his monovariant'); phrases such as 'similar to above', 'different from the others', 'I already addressed this in my previous post', 'as I said', 'the wiki solution #2', 'Solution 2', 'another way'; a reply that continues an argument the reader cannot see; and any sentence that would be incoherent if this were the first post. 0 = the post engages the bare problem as though nothing had been said yet; 10 = nearly every sentence leans on unseen prior posts. You must NOT judge whether back-reference is good, polite, helpful or lazy, must NOT judge the mathematics, and must NOT try to guess what the earlier posts said. Score only the visible extent of back-reference language.
proposals.rationale: Arrival position is not approach-match, but it leaves a loud lexical trace and plausibly co-varies with how a post is scored by a text-only model. R41 opens '@above that is listing everything out', R46 opens '@above thanks!', R14 is entirely a reply ('Um no, I already addressed this in my previous post'), R43 says 'here's my solution similar to above', R36 says 'I am confused on the wiki solution #2', and R03 self-describes as 'different from the others'. None of these markers is evidence about which route the write-up takes; they are timestamps in disguise. Tagged mixed because a poster arriving late may also genuinely be pushed toward an off-canonical route.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (how late in a decade-long thread the post arrived)

proposals.name: Legacy autocorrupted LaTeX and era-marked forum markup
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post carries typographic markers of an older era of this forum's software, judged purely by their presence. Count: math macros of the form backslash-equal-brace-brace and backslash-minus-brace-brace appearing where a plain equals sign or minus sign belongs; a stray space immediately after an opening dollar sign (for example a dollar sign followed by space then a numeral); bracketed url tags with a full http address inside the prose; double-square-bracket wiki-style links or File inclusions; hide tags whose argument is wrapped in double quotes rather than bare; and other markup that is not the modern plain form. 0 = none of these appear; 10 = they appear throughout. Do NOT judge whether old or new markup is better, cleaner or more readable, and do NOT judge the mathematics. Score only how much era-marked markup is visibly present.
proposals.rationale: Pure dating artifact with zero bearing on which solution route is taken. R01 contains both the corrupted equals macro and a bracketed http url tag; R14 contains the corrupted minus and equals macros; R12 and R35 show the spaced-dollar-sign habit of the same period. A text-only model can read the decade off these tokens, so they are a live nuisance channel; nothing about them says anything about approach.
proposals.upstream_parent: the calendar era in which the post was written (and later software migrations that rewrote old posts)

proposals.name: Density of display mathematics and align environments
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much of this post's mathematics is set as centred display or in multi-line aligned environments rather than run inline inside sentences. Consider the proportion of equations that are broken out on their own lines, the use of aligned/align-star or eqnarray blocks, chains of implication set on separate display lines, and tabular blocks. 0 = all mathematics is inline within running prose; 10 = the post is essentially a stack of display blocks with connective text between them. Do NOT judge whether the typesetting is attractive, readable or appropriate, and do NOT judge whether the mathematics is right. Score only the extent of display-versus-inline setting.
proposals.rationale: Typesetting habit tracks how much the author has written in this format before, not which route the argument takes. R05 and R45 set nearly every step in aligned blocks, and R57 does the same, while R08 and R27 present essentially identical kinds of reasoning entirely inline (R27 even in lowercase running prose). The two presentations of the same manipulations should not be distinguished by an approach-match target, so any predictive power here is nuisance. Tagged mixed because practised typesetters are also practised solvers.
proposals.upstream_parent: the poster's practice and fluency with the forum's typesetting conventions

proposals.name: Solution body wrapped in hide or spoiler blocks
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the substantive content of this post is enclosed in hide/spoiler wrappers rather than shown openly. Consider whether a hide tag exists at all, how much of the total text sits inside it, whether the wrapper carries a title such as 'Solution', 'sketch', 'what I did' or a jokey label, and whether multiple hidden blocks are nested inside the argument. 0 = nothing is hidden; 10 = the entire body is inside hide blocks. Do NOT judge whether hiding is courteous, evasive or good practice, and do NOT judge the content inside. Score only how much of the post is wrapped.
proposals.rationale: The wrapper is a courtesy convention about spoiling, orthogonal to which route is inside it. R18, R24, R29, R31, R35, R39, R48, R49 and R58 all bury the body in a hide block, several with editorial titles ('what I did', 'sketch', 'fakesolve', 'very cheap but fast solution'), while R06, R33 and R56 present the same kind of argument openly. R15 hides the mathematics and leaves the chatter outside, showing the wrapper is a layout decision, not a content one.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience norms and posting recency (hiding is the convention when readers may still be attempting the problem)

proposals.name: Casual affect, interjections and self-deprecating chatter
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much informal emotional register appears in the post: exclamations about the problem ('nice problem', 'holy cow'), emoticons or smilies, internet abbreviations and slang ('ngl', 'rip', 'fr', 'bro', 'bash'), lowercase-only stretches, filler or throwaway lines unrelated to the argument, self-mockery about one's own ability or process, and asides about how the poster felt while solving. 0 = the post is entirely impersonal and businesslike; 10 = affective chatter pervades it. Do NOT judge whether the informality is charming, unprofessional or distracting, and do NOT judge the mathematics. Score only how much of this register is visibly present.
proposals.rationale: Register is set by who the author imagines reading, which is an audience fact, not an approach fact. R17 opens 'Holy cow this configuration is so nice', R13 opens 'Very nice problem ngl' with a smiley, R53 is almost entirely lament ('rip me fr'), R43 opens 'Dangit this felt surprisingly hard or maybe I am just dumb', R15 closes with 'surprisingly this was the first solution i thought of', R55 closes with 'hmmm very algebraic in nature', and R10 opens with the placeholder word 's t o r a g e'. Stripping these lines would not change the route any of these posts takes.
proposals.upstream_parent: the poster's audience — peers reading in real time versus a stranger arriving later by search

proposals.name: Contest-provenance and collaboration framing
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post frames itself by the circumstances of its own production rather than by its content: statements that this was written during or just after the contest, references to a score or grade received, worry about points lost, elapsed solving time, comparisons to other problems on the same paper, and named co-solvers or credited collaborators ('Solved with ...', a bolded handle). 0 = no such framing anywhere; 10 = the post is dominated by it. Do NOT judge whether such framing is impressive, boastful or irrelevant, and do NOT treat any claimed score or timing as evidence of anything. Score only how much production-circumstance framing is visible.
proposals.rationale: This is a fingerprint of when the post was written and who the author knows, both unseen and both outside the target. R03 opens 'My solution during the contest (different from the others)', R22 opens 'Here is my solution during the contest', R26 opens 'Here is my cursed solution which somehow got a 7/7', R12 frets 'I'm hoping its not more than 1 point off', R32 reports 'It took ~1.3 hours. Meanwhile I thought #4 was far harder', and R37 and R55 both open with bolded co-solver credits. Tagged mixed because contestants who post immediately with credited collaborators are often strong solvers.
proposals.upstream_parent: timing of the post relative to the competition, plus the author's social embedding on the forum

proposals.name: Self-labelled deviation, cheapness or overkill
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how strongly the post advertises, in its own words, that it is unusual relative to whatever else exists: labels such as 'oversimplified', 'troll', 'scuffed', 'cheap but fast', 'fakesolve', 'cursed', 'overkill', 'ridiculous', 'a different solution for those who ...', 'not recognizing the standard idea, I did ...', or a title promising an alternative route. Score only the presence and prominence of the self-label. You must NOT attempt to verify the claim, must NOT compare the post to any other solution or document (you have not been shown any), and must NOT judge whether the label is accurate, modest or attention-seeking. 0 = the post makes no claim about its own unusualness; 10 = such a claim is the headline of the post.
proposals.rationale: A self-applied novelty label is a marketing act driven by thread position, not an observable property of the route, and a text-only model can read the label directly. R40 opens 'Oversimplified solution:', R28 opens 'Scuffed troll solution:', R24 titles its hide block 'very cheap but fast solution', R48 opens 'A different solution for those who understand less about complex numbers', R21 titles its hide block 'ridiculous and yet ultimately equivalent ... overkill', and R49 titles itself 'fakesolve'. Tagged mixed because a poster who says they went off-piste sometimes did.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream (the pressure on a later poster to advertise that they add something the thread lacks)

proposals.name: Tutorial-report register with numbered bolded section headings
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the post is organised as a formal report for a reader rather than as a working write-up: numbered and bolded section headings that name stages ('1. The Strategy', '2. Constructing ...', 'Conclusion'), a restatement of the goal before each stage, explicit signposting ('We now prove that', 'Let us evaluate', 'This implies that'), every routine algebraic step spelled out rather than compressed, and a closing paragraph that restates what was shown. 0 = no sectioning or signposting at all; 10 = fully sectioned, signposted and summarised. Do NOT judge whether this organisation is clear, bloated or professional, and do NOT judge the mathematics. Score only the extent of the report scaffolding.
proposals.rationale: Heavy report scaffolding is a trace of an editing process applied after the mathematics was fixed, so it can move a text-only model without any change of route. R13 is fully sectioned ('1. The Pigeonhole Strategy', '2. Constructing the Triplet', '3. Bounding the Sequence', '4. Covering all n', 'Conclusion') and restates its own goal three times; R30 and R39 use ruled separators and formally numbered Claims and Lemmas with restated statements. Compare R51 and R56, which carry out closely comparable constructions with no scaffolding at all. Tagged mixed because people who polish also often solve carefully.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing or assistance before posting (post-hoc polishing, or drafting help)

proposals.name: Help-seeking and uncertainty posture toward one's own post
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the post positions itself as unfinished or in need of confirmation: direct questions to readers ('Does this work?', 'Can someone please explain why ... is incorrect?', 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?', 'Did anyone else miss this?'), hedged self-report of a result ('I'm getting ...', 'I think ...', 'I hope it is valid'), a narrated attempt that stops before finishing, and admissions of a gap or an abandoned computation. 0 = the post asserts its content flatly with no appeal to the reader; 10 = it is principally a request for help or reassurance. Do NOT judge whether the uncertainty is warranted, humble or annoying, and do NOT decide whether the mathematics is correct. Score only the extent of the visible uncertainty posture.
proposals.rationale: Confidence of address is a fact about the author's experience and the conversational moment, not about which route the post takes. R44 opens 'Does this work?', R31 opens 'I'm getting 391' and closes 'Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?', R36 opens 'I am confused on the wiki solution #2' and closes 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?', R32 hopes 'I sure do hope it is valid', and R12 asks 'Did anyone else miss this?'. R59 narrates an attempt that was abandoned halfway. Tagged mixed because inexperienced posters may also more often be off the canonical route.
proposals.upstream_parent: the poster's standing and seniority on the forum, and their practice in this format

proposals.name: Answer-extraction framing versus proof framing in the item
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which this item is framed as short answer-extraction rather than as sustained proof. Consider both halves of what you are shown: whether the problem block displays a lettered option bank (A) through (E) or asks for a single numeric quantity such as m+n, and whether the post terminates in a boxed or lettered final answer, uses phrasing like 'the answer is' or 'our answer is', reasons by elimination among the given options, or resolves in a handful of lines. 0 = an open-ended prove-or-show item answered by extended argument; 10 = an option-bank or numeric-answer item resolved to a boxed answer. Do NOT judge whether short answers or long proofs are better, harder or more valuable, and do NOT judge correctness. Score only the extent of answer-extraction framing.
proposals.rationale: Problem kind is a property of the container the post landed in, not of the post's own approach, yet it is fully visible in the text and so is a strong text-only confound. R01, R23, R24, R28, R41, R48, R53 and R60 all sit under lettered option banks and end in a lettered or boxed answer, and R50 and R58 resolve numeric-answer items in a few lines; R02, R30, R32, R39 and R42 sit under 'Prove that' or 'Show that' statements with no answer to extract. Tagged mixed because the number of genuinely distinct viable routes really does depend on problem kind.
proposals.upstream_parent: the kind of problem the thread is attached to (short computational contest question with one obvious route versus hard olympiad problem drawing many attacks)

proposals.name: Isolable pivotal-fact statement
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post states a single crisp pivotal identity, lemma, or structural fact as a self-contained claim that could stand alone as the crux of a solution, independent of whether surrounding derivation or final computation is completed. A 10: a specific formula/identity/lemma is explicitly isolated and named as the key fact (e.g., stated on its own line or flagged as 'the key point is...'), even if little else is derived. A 0: no such isolable pivotal fact ever appears; the post is either a diffuse mass of computation with no single fact singled out, or contains no mathematical content at all.
proposals.rationale: R52 states only the monovariant idea ('the difference between the largest and smallest a_i') without any write-up, and R59 states only the identity F_2n/F_n = F_{n+1}+F_{n-1} without deriving it or finishing the computation; both are terse to the point of being unfinished, yet both carry dense_pct far above card_pct, suggesting the dense model credits a correctly isolated crux fact even when nothing else is shown.

proposals.name: Unresolved doubt about correctness
proposals.instruction: Score how much the post leaves the correctness of an approach or answer (its own, or another poster's) openly unresolved by ending in a question or explicit doubt rather than a settled claim. A 10: the post commits to its claims throughout and never asks the reader to confirm or explain whether something is right or wrong. A 0: the post's substantive content is framed as, or ends with, an unresolved question about correctness (e.g., 'wouldn't that be overcounting?', 'can someone explain why X is incorrect?').
proposals.rationale: R05 is built entirely around doubting the wiki solution ('Wouldn't that be overcounting?') and R60 ends with 'Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?' after presenting a full derivation; both have among the lowest dense_pct in the slice (0.206, 0.161) despite substantial card_pct, suggesting the dense model discounts posts that end without committing to their own correctness.

proposals.name: Named theorem as embedded step vs. sole content
proposals.instruction: Score how a named classical theorem, competition lemma, or closed-form formula (if the post uses one at all) functions within the solution. A 10: the named theorem/formula appears as one supporting step embedded inside a longer argument that also independently derives problem-specific structure from scratch (new points, algebraic identities, casework, etc.). A 0: the entire substantive content of the post is 'cite the named theorem/formula, then substitute the problem's specific numbers,' with no other derivation of why or how it applies. If no named theorem is invoked at all, score based on whether the solution is nonetheless built from an unexplained black-box step (0) or a from-scratch derivation (10).
proposals.rationale: R23 (cites the hook-length formula and plugs in numbers, nothing else) and R26 (cites Minkowski's inequality and squares/solves, nothing else) both sit at the black-box end with low dense_pct (0.254, 0.268) and very high card_pct; by contrast R48 (Miquel's Theorem and Radical Axes used as intermediate steps inside a longer chain of claims) and R50 (Cauchy-Schwarz equality case used inside a longer incenter-touch-point setup) sit at the embedded-step end with high dense_pct (0.762, 0.865) and low card_pct.

proposals.name: Self-labels own method as hacky or non-rigorous
proposals.instruction: Score whether the poster explicitly characterizes their own method, in their own words, as a shortcut, hack, guess, or non-genuine solve (e.g., 'troll solution', 'fakesolve', 'cheap but fast', 'ridiculous... overkill', 'scuffed'). A 10: the post never characterizes its own technique this way; it is presented (rightly or wrongly) as a genuine solution. A 0: the poster explicitly flags their own approach with this kind of self-deprecating or hedging label.
proposals.rationale: R12 opens with 'Scuffed troll solution', R53 is tagged '[hide=fakesolve]', R39 calls its own method 'ridiculous and yet ultimately equivalent... overkill', and R7 is labeled a 'cheap but fast solution' — all four carry unusually low dense_pct (0.274, 0.056, 0.140, 0.324, respectively) despite mostly high card_pct, a consistent pattern across four separate rows.

proposals.name: Generalizes beyond the minimum needed
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post goes beyond exactly what is needed to answer the stated problem, e.g. by extending the argument to a broader family (different n, different configuration), stating additional properties of the configuration, or adding a labeled 'further observations' section. A 10: the post clearly extends its reasoning or findings beyond the minimal answer, with the extension clearly marked as bonus/general material. A 0: the post stops the instant the requested quantity is obtained, with no exploration of the broader structure.
proposals.rationale: R20 solves the specific 10-move triangle question quickly, then extends its method to general n-gon random walks and takes a limit as k→∞; R48 answers the requested AB^2 and then adds an 'Other Observations' section on the K-symmedian and the P-Dumpty point. Both carry high dense_pct (0.865, 0.762) despite low card_pct.

proposals.name: Small-case tabulation leading to general proof
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post computes/tabulates several small explicit cases, states an observed pattern from that table, and then proves the pattern holds in general (typically by induction). A 10: an explicit small-case table or list is shown, a pattern is named from it, and the pattern is then proved in general. A 0: no small-case exploration appears; the post either jumps directly to a general argument or gives no argument at all.
proposals.rationale: Both independent solutions to the powers-of-2 representation-count problem, R42 and R45, build a table of f(0) through f(7), observe that f(2^a - 1) is exactly the odd values, and then prove this by strong induction; both carry unusually high dense_pct (0.921 and 0.972, the latter one of the highest in the whole slice) despite modest card_pct.

proposals.name: Formal discrete Claim/Proof micro-structure
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post breaks its argument into explicitly labeled, individually closed sub-claims (e.g., 'Claim: ... Proof: ... [box/qed]', numbered or colored claim headers), each proved separately, rather than presenting one continuous unstructured block of reasoning. A 10: multiple discrete labeled claims are stated and each is closed with its own proof/qed marker. A 0: the argument is one continuous block with no labeled sub-claims.
proposals.rationale: R15 breaks its geometry solution into six separately labeled 'Claim... Proof...' blocks each closed with a black square, and R33 breaks its number-theory solution into headed sections ('1. The Pigeonhole Strategy', '2. Constructing the Triplet', etc.) each with its own closed argument; both carry high dense_pct (0.792 and 0.889).

proposals.name: Shown-work density in computation
proposals.instruction: Score how much of the algebraic/arithmetic work needed to reach the final claims is actually displayed step-by-step, versus compressed into phrases like 'this simplifies to', 'clearly', or 'it can easily be checked' with the intermediate steps omitted. A 10: essentially all intermediate algebraic/arithmetic steps needed to verify the claims are shown explicitly. A 0: key steps are skipped and asserted via hand-wave phrases, forcing the reader to redo the algebra themselves.
proposals.rationale: R33 shows every intermediate step of the interval-overlap and quadratic-root computation in full; contrast R43, which states only the final binomial-coefficient formula and its numeric evaluation with zero shown steps ('$\frac{\binom{5}{2}-\binom{3}{2}}{\binom{5}{2}}=\frac{7}{10}$'). R33 has dense_pct 0.889 and card_pct 0.293, while R43 has dense_pct 0.432 and card_pct 0.995, the single highest card_pct in the entire 60-row slice.

proposals.name: Explicit reduction to a cleaner equivalent sub-problem
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post explicitly recognizes and states that the given problem is equivalent to, or reducible to, a cleaner restated sub-problem, and then solves that restated version instead of working directly with the original phrasing throughout. A 10: the post explicitly states an equivalence/reduction ('it suffices to find...', 'this turns into a problem where...') and then solves the restated version. A 0: the post works with the problem exactly as originally phrased from start to finish, with no explicit reduction step.
proposals.rationale: R33 explicitly reduces the card-pile problem to 'it suffices to find a triplet of distinct integers... such that all three pairwise sums... are perfect squares,' and R41 explicitly reduces the disjoint-triangles probability problem to 'a problem where you want to find the number of ways that A, B, and C are together in a circular arrangement of ABCDEF.' Both carry high dense_pct (0.889 and 0.911) with low card_pct.

proposals.name: Redundant cross-checked derivation of the same quantity
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post derives the same intermediate quantity via two independently structured routes and then sets the two results equal (or checks they agree) as a way of pinning down or confirming the answer, versus deriving each needed quantity only once. A 10: at least one quantity is explicitly computed two different ways and the two results are compared/equated. A 0: every quantity in the solution is computed exactly once, with no redundant cross-check.
proposals.rationale: R58 computes f(f(f(x))) two separate ways (via the identity on f(x) directly, and via first computing f(f(x)) then applying f again) and equates the results to finish the proof; R24 does the identical double-computation of f(f(f(x))) for the same reason. R58 has the highest dense_pct in the entire slice (0.994) and R24 is also high (0.921), both with low card_pct.

proposals.name: Self-aware contrast against a standard or alternate approach
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post explicitly signals awareness of a different, more standard, or more laborious alternate approach and positions its own method as deliberately different from or cleaner than that alternative (e.g., 'solution without the pointwise trap', 'I thought I'd try something bashy instead but no'). A 10: the post explicitly names or gestures at an alternate approach and contrasts its own method against it. A 0: the post gives no indication that any alternate approach exists or was considered.
proposals.rationale: R44 is explicitly titled 'Solution without pointwise trap' and separately notes the multiple co-solvers who worked out the cleaner route; R34 remarks 'surprisingly this was the first solution i thought of, i thought i'd figure out something real bashy instead but nah.' Both carry high dense_pct (0.844 and 0.778) with low card_pct.

proposals.name: Names and separately addresses a trap or edge case
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post explicitly names a specific trap, degenerate configuration, or edge case (rather than only implicitly handling it inside general casework) and pauses to address it as its own labeled step. A 10: a specific trap/edge case is explicitly named (e.g., 'the pointwise trap', 'if a=b this fails', 'the degenerate case where...') and separately resolved. A 0: no edge case or trap is ever explicitly named as such, even if some casework is present.
proposals.rationale: R24 has a section explicitly headed 'We now deal with the pointwise trap' with three enumerated subcases; R31 structures its final claims (Claims 2-4) explicitly around ruling out specific degenerate value-pairings the pointwise ambiguity could produce. Both carry high dense_pct (0.921 and 0.817) with low card_pct.

proposals.name: Ties the final quantity to an interpretive meaning
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post, at the point of concluding, explicitly explains what the final computed number or object represents in terms of the problem's original request, rather than ending on a bare formula or numeral. A 10: the post has an explicit closing statement connecting the final computation back to the specific thing the problem asked for. A 0: the post ends on a bare number, formula, or boxed expression with no closing interpretive sentence.
proposals.rationale: R33 closes with an explicit 'Conclusion' paragraph restating exactly why the covering-interval argument answers the pigeonhole requirement for all n; R48 closes with 'Other Observations' explicitly interpreting the found relations (e.g., that XY bisects angle CXD, that X is a P-Dumpty point). Both carry high dense_pct (0.889, 0.762) with low card_pct.

proposals.name: Direct derivation vs. contradiction-hypothesis framing
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post's main proof architecture is a direct forward derivation of necessary conditions versus one built around explicitly assuming the negation of the desired conclusion and deriving an impossibility (e.g., 'FTSOC', 'suppose for the sake of contradiction', 'assume otherwise, then...'). A 10: the argument proceeds as a direct chain of forward implications with no reliance on an assumed-false hypothesis as its central device. A 0: the central structural move is an explicit contradiction hypothesis that is carried through to a derived impossibility.
proposals.rationale: On the identical problem (2^n+12^n+2011^n a perfect square), R01 is built around 'FTSOC $2^n+12^n+2011^n$ is a perfect square for some $n\geq2$' and derives a contradiction, while R10 argues directly and forward via a single mod-12 quadratic-residue computation with no contradiction hypothesis at all. R01 has dense_pct 0.361 and card_pct 0.999; R10 has dense_pct 0.792 and card_pct 0.197 — the two solve the same problem but sit at opposite ends of both scales.

proposals.name: Introduces new auxiliary objects tied explicitly to the problem
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post explicitly defines new auxiliary points, objects, or variables that do not appear in the original problem statement, with a clear stated tie to the problem's given quantities, before carrying out the main derivation. A 10: at least one clearly defined new auxiliary object/variable is introduced and explicitly tied to the given configuration, and becomes load-bearing in the argument. A 0: the solution works only with the objects and variables exactly as given in the problem statement, introducing no new auxiliary construction.
proposals.rationale: R50 opens by defining new touch-point variables x=AE=AF, y=BF=BD, z=CD=CE tied to the incenter of the triangle before any manipulation begins; R38 defines a new point T (intersection of the tangents to (ABC) at B and C) before starting its angle chase. Both carry high dense_pct (0.865 and 0.833) with low card_pct.

proposals.name: Self-deprecating/hedging authorial tone
proposals.instruction: Read only the post text. Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the author uses self-deprecating, hedging, or uncertainty-signaling language about their own solution or competence (e.g. 'not sure', 'I sure do hope it is valid', 'scuffed', 'oversimplified', 'cheap', admissions of confusion, sad/frustrated emoticons). 0 = no such language anywhere; 10 = pervasive self-deprecation or hedging throughout the post. Do NOT judge whether the solution is actually good, rigorous, or correctly hedged -- score only how much of this self-referential hedging language is present in the text.
proposals.rationale: Hedging register shows up on both sides of the split (R13, R22, R39 are dense_high_card_low; R24, R34, R56, R60 are dense_low_card_high), so it plausibly tracks general disagreement/extremity rather than genuine approach-match, but an uncertain author may also genuinely be groping toward a non-canonical route, so it is not purely a nuisance.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's confidence and self-presentation practice in this format

proposals.name: Formal Claim/Proof macro & color-markup density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post uses structured presentation macros: [color=...] tags, bolded/labeled 'Claim'/'Proof'/'Lemma' headers, numbered section headers (e.g. '1. ...', '2. ...'), or repeated boxed-answer formatting used as a structuring device. 0 = plain unstructured prose with none of these; 10 = heavy, systematic use of colored/labeled/numbered macro structure throughout. Do not judge whether the structure is helpful or well-organized -- score only how much of this specific markup vocabulary appears.
proposals.rationale: R28 and R44/R59 are saturated with numbered/colored Claim-Proof macros while short posts like R36 and R53 have none, so this tracks presentation fluency; it is mixed because authors fluent enough to deploy formal Claim/Proof scaffolding may also be more likely to reconstruct the textbook-style steps that match a canonical editorial derivation.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practiced typographic/markup habit in this venue (formatting seniority)

proposals.name: Named collaborator/co-solver byline
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post text explicitly credits or names other forum users as co-solvers or collaborators (e.g. 'Solved with X', naming specific handles as partners in producing the write-up). 0 = no such credit given anywhere; 10 = prominent, explicit collaborator crediting. Do not judge whether the collaboration produced a stronger or weaker solution -- score only whether this crediting language is present.
proposals.rationale: R14 ('Solved with S.Ragnork1729, SilverBlaze_SY and HACK_IN_MATHS') and R57 ('Solved with mathapple101') both carry this byline; it is mixed because group-vetted solutions may genuinely converge more often on the standard/canonical route via peer correction.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's social network / collaborative solving culture

proposals.name: Backward reference to earlier thread activity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post's language presupposes that earlier posts or other users' work already exist in this thread -- e.g. '@[username]', 'as above', 'similar to what was posted', naming another poster's reasoning by handle, directly replying to or quoting a prior post. 0 = the post reads as if it is the first entry, engaging only the bare problem; 10 = the post is saturated with references to prior posts or users. Do not judge whether the referenced material is used correctly -- score only the presence of this backward-referencing language.
proposals.rationale: R08 ('@above thanks!'), R30 ('@above that is listing everything out...'), and R04 ('reasoning similar to Altheman's') all show this fingerprint; it is mixed because a late arrival that has read earlier posts (possibly including one matching the canonical approach) may genuinely be more likely to adopt that same approach.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream -- the post arrived after others and shows it

proposals.name: Explicit alternative/numbered-solution self-labeling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post explicitly labels itself as an additional, later, or alternative solution relative to others already in the thread -- phrases like 'Solution 2', 'a different solution', 'another way', 'my solution during the contest (different from the others)'. 0 = no such self-labeling anywhere; 10 = the post is framed centrally around declaring itself an alternate or later entry. Do not judge whether the alternative is actually different in substance -- score only the presence of this self-labeling language.
proposals.rationale: R31 ('A different solution for those who understand less about complex numbers...') and R45/R46 ('My solution during the contest (different from the others)'/'with bit modifications') show this framing explicitly; it is mixed because an author who flags their entry as 'different' is plausibly also more likely to actually have taken a non-canonical route, which is close to the real construct.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream / awareness that other solutions already exist

proposals.name: Competition-math community shorthand/jargon density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post uses insider community shorthand without explanation -- e.g. 'WLOG', 'FTSOC', 'Let P(x,y) denote the assertion', named recurring-trick labels like 'pointwise trap', forum-specific emoticons (e.g. :yoda:, :blacksquare:). 0 = no such shorthand, everything spelled out in plain language; 10 = jargon-dense throughout. Do not judge whether the jargon is used correctly or reflects real expertise -- score only how much of this shorthand vocabulary appears.
proposals.rationale: The 'P(x,y) denote the assertion' / 'pointwise trap' shorthand recurs across the repeated functional-equation item (R14, R40, R47, R58), all dense_high_card_low; it is mixed because seniority that produces this jargon fluency may also make an author more likely to reproduce the standard/canonical derivation steps.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice and seniority within this specific competition-math subculture

proposals.name: Contest-time vs. after-the-fact production self-report
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post explicitly situates its own production in time relative to the contest -- phrases like 'during the contest', 'on the test', a labeled problem tag like 'p9:', reporting a live score like 'got a 7/7', or otherwise narrating the real-time experience of solving under contest conditions. 0 = no temporal self-report of this kind; 10 = the post is framed heavily around this contest-time narration. Do not judge whether the solution is more or less rigorous as a result -- score only the presence of this self-reported timing language.
proposals.rationale: R08 ('p9: We have...') and R47 ('cursed solution which somehow got a 7/7') report contest-time production, as do R45/R46 ('my solution during the contest'); it is mixed because time-pressured contest attempts may genuinely diverge from (or converge with) the polished editorial route more than leisurely after-the-fact write-ups do.
proposals.upstream_parent: timing of production (live contest attempt vs. later leisure engagement)

proposals.name: Feedback-soliciting address to the audience
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post text directly solicits a response, correction, or confirmation from readers rather than presenting a self-contained finished write-up -- e.g. 'Can someone please explain...', 'Did anyone else miss this?', 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?', 'Does this work?'. 0 = the post makes no request for reader input; 10 = the post is centrally framed as a question or request for feedback. Do not judge whether the underlying solution is complete or correct -- score only the presence of this feedback-soliciting address.
proposals.rationale: R43 ('Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?') and R24 ('Wouldn't that be overcounting?') both close on a request for confirmation rather than a settled write-up; R37 ('Did anyone else miss this?') does the same -- this address-to-audience framing is orthogonal to which solution route was actually taken.
proposals.upstream_parent: process dynamics on the receiving side / author's intent to solicit peer feedback rather than deliver a finished write-up

proposals.name: Raw verbosity/length of the post
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post is long and elaborated versus short and compressed, judged purely by the amount of running text and number of displayed equations or steps (not by whether that length is well-organized or necessary). 0 = a one- or two-line post; 10 = an extremely long, many-step, many-display-equation post. Do not judge whether the length is warranted or the extra material is useful -- score only the raw amount of text.
proposals.rationale: R41 and R44 run to many paragraphs and displayed lemma chains while R36, R53, and R54 are a sentence or two; length is a pure surface proxy that can move a text-perception dense model without tracking whether the approach matches the editorial.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Explicit citation of or engagement with an external/wiki reference
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post text itself names or links to an outside reference -- e.g. an embedded [url=...] link, the phrase 'wiki solution', 'the wiki', or otherwise explicitly naming an external write-up it is drawing on or questioning. 0 = no such citation anywhere in the text; 10 = the post is centrally built around naming or quoting an external reference. Do not judge whether the citation is accurate or the linked material authoritative -- score only whether this citing language appears in the text.
proposals.rationale: R21 embeds a '[url=...Young_tableau...]hook-length formula[/url]' link and R24 opens with 'I am confused on the wiki solution #2 for this' -- both are textual, in-post citations (not judge-side comparisons); it is mixed because a post that explicitly engages the wiki write-up may also be more likely to actually track its approach.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's engagement with existing reference material (linking to or questioning the wiki)

proposals.name: Pivotal idea named in standard terms, execution aside
proposals.instruction: Score how explicitly the post names the single structural fact, object, or technique on which the problem turns, using vocabulary a reader of this subject would recognize, independently of whether the post carries the work through. 10: the crux is stated outright in one recognizable sentence -- a named identity, a monovariant, a configuration assumption, an auxiliary point, an invariant -- even if the post then stops mid-way, rambles, gives no arithmetic and no final answer. 5: the crux is implicit in the manipulations and a reader could name it, but the post never says it. 0: the post produces output without ever articulating a crux -- pure computation, pure narration of the poster's feelings, or a chain of steps from which no nameable pivotal idea can be extracted.
proposals.rationale: R08 contains no completed computation at all yet names the crux assumption (the 1-2-sqrt5 triangles) in one line; R20 supplies nothing but the monovariant (difference between largest and smallest a_i) plus a caveat about it not decreasing every step; R27 states the identity F_2n/F_n = F_{n+1}+F_{n-1} and then abandons the problem entirely. A bank weighted on completeness, rigor or presentation must floor all three, yet the identifying idea is plainly on the page in each. This criterion separates possession of the idea from execution of it.

proposals.name: Construction and its validity range derived, not tuned
proposals.instruction: For posts that hinge on an explicit construction (a triple, a family, a substitution, a witness sequence), score jointly (a) whether the post shows where the construction comes from and (b) whether the range over which it works is established algebraically. 10: the construction is solved for out of the conditions it must satisfy (set up the required equations, invert them to get the object), and the range of parameters is derived by an explicit inequality or covering argument. 5: one of the two halves is done (derived object with hand-checked range, or conjured object with derived range). 0: the object appears from nowhere ('consider the triple ...', 'I claim these numbers work') and its applicability is patched by hand-listed numeric special cases or a single verified instance.
proposals.rationale: Five posts in the slice attack the same cards-and-perfect-squares problem with essentially the same triple. R60 sets up x+y, y+z, x+z as three consecutive squares, solves the linear system to produce the triple, then derives the interval overlap condition m^2-8m-3 >= 0 and the covering threshold 99. R29 asserts the identical triple with no derivation; R02 patches the small range with two hand-tuned windows (100-126 via (126,163,198) and 127-144 via (160,201,240)); R06 hand-checks n <= 107 with x=9. R15 likewise conjures the scaling a^4 b^3 x_i with no account of where it came from.

proposals.name: Argument stays in the problem's native framework
proposals.instruction: Score whether the argument is conducted in the same kind of objects the problem statement is phrased in, versus transported wholesale into a different computational framework and settled there. 10: a synthetic configuration problem is settled by synthetic reasoning about that configuration; a counting problem by counting arguments; a number-theory problem by number-theoretic structure. 3: a foreign framework is used for one auxiliary step inside otherwise native reasoning. 0: the entire problem is immediately recast into coordinates, the complex plane, a finite field, a graph, or a generating function, and the original objects never reappear except in the final answer.
proposals.rationale: R26 tosses an incenter-and-arc-midpoint configuration onto the complex unit circle and reduces the whole problem to checking one ratio is real; R37 evaluates a complex-number expression inside F_25 because the answer choices survive the transport; R46 replaces an angle-between-two-slopes question with coordinate verification that a specific triangle is right isosceles; R14 replaces the cards problem with bipartiteness of an explicitly built graph and an odd 7-cycle. Contrast R19, R38 and R57, which stay entirely inside the circle-and-angle language of their statements.

proposals.name: Computes the asked quantity rather than eliminating options
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post determines the requested quantity on its own terms or instead exploits the presence of a finite option list. 10: the post derives the value or proves the statement without ever using the answer choices; the argument would read identically if the choices were deleted. 5: the choices are used only as a final sanity check on an independently derived value. 0: the argument is elimination or localization -- parity, a small modulus, an approximation, a single falsifying instance -- that is only sufficient because the options are given, and would not determine the answer if they were removed.
proposals.rationale: R23 computes only the parity and the residue mod 3 of f(2018) and picks the one choice that is odd and 1 mod 3; R03 sets a^2 = ab = b^2 to get an approximate 72 and then reads off nearby prime pairs; R42 exhibits the all-draw tournament purely to falsify option E; R05 grinds twelve powers of z by hand rather than using the structure. In every case the post is efficient, correct and cleanly boxed -- exactly what a rubric of criteria rewards -- while the reasoning route is one the problem's own statement does not license.

proposals.name: Advertises itself as a departure from the usual treatment
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the post signals, in its own words, that its method is unusual, alternative, or different from what is normally done or from what other posters did. 10: an explicit departure claim -- 'instead of the usual X I used Y', 'a different solution', 'not recognizing X, I came up with overkill', 'different from the others' -- appears in the post. 5: a softer signal of idiosyncrasy such as remarking on the flavor of the method after the fact. 0: no such signal, or the post presents its route as the ordinary thing to do.
proposals.rationale: R14 says outright 'Instead of the usual three number construction, I used seven numbers' and hides the whole post under 'different from the others'; R37 opens 'Not recognizing the root of unity, I came up with ridiculous and yet ultimately equivalent overkill'; R05 opens 'A different solution for those who understand less about complex numbers'; R02 closes with 'hmmm very algebraic in nature'. These self-reports are direct textual evidence about which route the author took, cost nothing to judge, and are the kind of surface signal an explicitly written criterion bank has no reason to contain.

proposals.name: Disclaims the legitimacy of its own method
proposals.instruction: Score the degree to which the post labels its own method as illegitimate, cheap, fake, or a shortcut, as distinct from labelling it merely ugly or long. 10: an explicit legitimacy disclaimer -- 'fakesolve', 'troll solution', 'very cheap but fast', 'oversimplified' -- attached to the method itself. 5: a self-deprecating remark about style or length only ('cursed', 'bashy', 'storage'), with the method presented as genuinely valid. 0: the post presents its argument as a complete and legitimate proof with no disclaimer.
proposals.rationale: R26 is filed under 'fakesolve'; R03 opens 'Scuffed troll solution'; R23 hides under 'very cheap but fast solution'; R12 opens 'Oversimplified solution'. Separating this from mere self-deprecation matters: R36 calls itself a 'cursed solution' but immediately adds that it scored 7/7 and then executes a full case analysis, and R44 is headed 's t o r a g e' while containing a complete case argument. A criterion that lumps all self-deprecation together would mis-score those two; this one asks specifically whether the author is disavowing the validity of the route.

proposals.name: Canonical opening moves, taken in the canonical order
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post's first several steps are the moves the problem type ordinarily invites, taken in the ordinary order, versus exotic openings. For a functional equation: substituting zero, substituting the simplest arguments, comparing an assertion with its sign-flipped or swapped version, extracting parity or evenness -- taken early. 10: the first three or four moves are all of this ordinary kind and each is a plain substitution into the given relation. 5: an ordinary opening followed by an exotic middle. 0: the post opens with a bespoke substitution of a rational expression in the variables, subtracts one instantiation of the assertion from another, or immediately changes variables into a newly defined function, before the elementary substitutions have been exhausted.
proposals.rationale: R30, R32, R45 and R48 all open with P(0,0), P(x,0), P(x,x^2) or P(x,x^2/2), then compare P(x,y) with P(-x,y) to get evenness -- a shared elementary opening. R11 instead reaches immediately for P(u, u/(u-1)) and then redefines g(x)=f(x+1) to run the rest of the argument in g; R39 forms differences of assertions such as P(f(x),f(y)) minus P(x+1,y+1) and P(2-x,2-y) minus P(x,y). All four families are functional equations solved by substitution, so a bank measuring 'uses substitutions systematically' cannot separate them; the ordinariness of the particular substitutions can.

proposals.name: Bespoke machinery invented where off-the-shelf steps exist
proposals.instruction: Score how much new apparatus the post invents for its own use: new definitions, new named predicates, new notation, a reindexed auxiliary function, a translation into a structure not mentioned in the problem. 10: no invented apparatus; every step uses standard notions of the subject. 5: one convenient piece of local notation, introduced for brevity only. 0: the argument is built on two or more author-coined objects (a coined predicate, a coined auxiliary function, a coined counting scheme) and cannot be followed without adopting them.
proposals.rationale: R11 recasts everything through g(x)=f(x+1) and proves properties of g rather than f; R33 coins the predicate 'q is p-good' and builds two claims on it; R22 coins a partition into sets of sizes s_i, proves a bespoke binomial convexity lemma, and double counts against it; R14 coins a graph whose edges encode square sums. Invented apparatus is a strong visible marker and is orthogonal to rigor -- all four of these posts are rigorous -- so a bank scoring correctness and completeness will rate them highly while this property is invisible to it.

proposals.name: Intermediate results promoted to stated, proved claims
proposals.instruction: Score whether the load-bearing intermediate facts are lifted out and stated as standalone claims or lemmas with their own proofs, versus being consumed inline in a single compressed chain. 10: two or more intermediate facts are stated as claims in general form and each is proved separately before being used. 5: one such claim, or claims stated but proved only by a parenthetical. 0: the whole argument is one uninterrupted chain of implications with no fact ever isolated, however correct.
proposals.rationale: R17 states and proves four numbered claims; R19 states and proves five claims and then finishes by radical axis on the three circles it built; R24 states three lemmas before the case analysis. By contrast R10 disposes of its problem in four lines with two moduli and no isolated statement, and R51 is a single display line invoking Minkowski. Both compressed posts are correct and complete, so completeness-shaped criteria rate them well; whether the intermediate structure is exposed is a different property, and it is the one that visibly differs across this slice.

proposals.name: One cited heavyweight theorem does all the work
proposals.instruction: Score the extent to which the post's entire content is a single invocation of a named or linked heavy result, versus the use of named results as steps inside an argument the post itself builds. 10 (heavy end): the post is essentially one application of a named theorem or a linked formula, with no configuration built, no case analysis, and nothing left to do after the invocation. 5: a named result supplies the decisive step but the post sets up the objects it applies to and draws consequences after it. 0: the post builds its own chain and uses named results only as ordinary tools among many.
proposals.rationale: R49 is one line consisting of a Wikipedia link to the hook-length formula and the resulting fraction; R51 is one display line invoking Minkowski and reading off n=12; R52 asserts a per-term bound whose only justification is that a-b is a root of the difference. Contrast R43, which builds the intouch lengths x, y, z, rewrites the hypothesis, recognizes it as the equality case of Cauchy-Schwarz, and then extracts the ratio -- the named tool is a step, not the whole post. Both shapes are correct and both are concise, so length and correctness criteria cannot separate them.

proposals.name: Degenerate or pitfall branch identified and killed
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post recognizes the branch a careless argument would silently skip and disposes of it explicitly. 10: the post names the trap (a pointwise alternative, a division by a possibly-zero quantity, a boundary or equality case the problem explicitly asks about, a degenerate configuration) and closes it with an argument. 5: the trap is mentioned and dismissed with a one-line reason. 0: the trap is passed over silently, or a step that requires the trap to be absent is taken without comment.
proposals.rationale: R36 enumerates three cases of the pointwise trap with four subcases inside the third; R24 separately kills the branch where f vanishes at a nonzero point and the mixed-sign branch; R48 does the same in two paragraphs. Against them, R35 asserts convexity in each variable and stops at 'the maximum occurs on the boundary' without the equality determination the problem explicitly requests, and R52 never discusses equality either. The presence or absence of the skipped branch is judgeable from the post alone and is heavily concentrated on one side of this slice.

proposals.name: Polish and answer packaging out of proportion to idea content
proposals.instruction: Score the gap between how finished the post looks and how much reasoning it contains. 10: the post is highly packaged -- tidy formatting, a boxed or bolded final answer, no loose ends, confident closing -- while the reasoning it contains is a couple of lines or a lookup. 5: packaging proportionate to content. 0: the post is visibly unpackaged -- conversational, mid-thought, no final answer, no formatting -- whatever reasoning it does contain.
proposals.rationale: Written deliberately as an over-credit detector. R10, R21, R05 and R49 are all short, tidy, boxed and immediately readable, and a bank built from explicitly written criteria (clarity, completeness of presentation, presence of a final answer, correct notation) will reward each of them near the top. R08, R20 and R31 sit at the opposite extreme -- prose fragments, no final answer, no formatting -- and any such bank must floor them. Scoring the packaging axis on its own lets it be subtracted rather than absorbed.

proposals.name: Shows how the decisive move was found
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post exposes the discovery path -- data gathered, a pattern observed, a strategy announced before it is executed, a reason the particular move is the natural one -- as opposed to presenting only the finished chain. 10: the post computes small cases or states the plan, draws the conjecture from them, and only then proves it, so a reader could have found the move themselves. 5: a one-clause motivation attached to an otherwise finished chain. 0: the finished chain only; each step is verifiable but nothing indicates why it was chosen.
proposals.rationale: R56 tabulates f(0) through f(7), writes 'it seems like all f(2^a-1) are odd, so i will try proving that', and then proves it; R01 proves the recurrence by casework on the first summand before using it, so the recurrence is earned rather than quoted; R60 announces 'The Pigeonhole Strategy' and 'Constructing the Triplet' as headers before executing each. Against them R51 and R15 give only the finished object. Note that R56 and R01 solve the same problem and both sit high on the dense side while differing widely in polish, which suggests the discovery path rather than the polish is what is being tracked.

proposals.name: Post questions or disowns the argument it posts
proposals.instruction: Score the post's stance toward the reasoning it displays. 10: the post asserts its argument as correct and finished. 5: the post asserts the argument but hedges about a specific step. 0: the post displays reasoning it does not stand behind -- asks why its answer is wrong, asks whether the approach works, or reproduces someone else's argument in order to object to it.
proposals.rationale: R07 lays out a full derivation, reaches 391, and closes with 'Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?'; R58 reproduces a wiki argument and asks 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?'; R34 presents a two-case proof under the heading 'Does this work?'. A criterion bank scoring the mathematics on the page will read all three as substantial and largely well-formed, since the displayed work is long and structured, and will have no slot for the author's own repudiation of it.

proposals.name: Explores the configuration beyond the minimum needed
proposals.instruction: Score whether the post says more about the structure than the question required: an alternative route noted, a generalization carried out, extra properties of the configuration recorded, a remark on why the configuration behaves as it does. 10: the post finishes the question and then adds substantive further structure -- a general-parameter version, a list of further observations, or an explicitly named alternative method. 5: a single aside such as naming one other method that would also work. 0: the post stops the instant the question is answered.
proposals.rationale: R57 finishes and then adds an 'Other Observations' block on the symmedian, the ratio CY/YD, and the Dumpty point; R13 answers the ten-move question in one display and then develops the limiting distribution for a general n-gon with arbitrary step probabilities; R38 finishes and notes 'Instead of angle chasing, inversion would also work'. This surplus is not rewarded by anything a completeness- or efficiency-shaped criterion measures -- it is strictly beyond what was asked, and on an efficiency criterion it would be penalized -- yet it is a visible marker of how the author is holding the problem.

proposals.name: Compressed veteran register: terse, routine steps elided
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the post is written in a compressed, insider register: it does not restate or paraphrase the problem, it opens directly on a computation or a named tool, it compresses routine algebra into a single line or an implication chain, it uses standard-abbreviation shorthand (WLOG, FTSOC, QR, PIE, POP, mod, 'clearly', 'obviously', 'easily checked', 'we are done'), and it assumes the reader already knows the standard machinery. 0 = fully expanded, every step spelled out and motivated, nothing left to the reader; 10 = maximally clipped, whole routine stages replaced by a phrase or a single displayed line. Score only how much compression is PRESENT. You must NOT judge whether the compression is good, whether the gaps are legitimate, whether the argument is correct, or whether the post is easy to follow. Do not compare the post to any other document.
proposals.rationale: R05 and R34 dispatch an olympiad number-theory problem in three or four clipped lines with 'trivially works' / 'FTSOC'; R21 is a single Minkowski display plus a box; R47 is a five-line 'kills the problem' write-up. Against these, R14 and R39 narrate every substitution in longhand. Register-of-compression is a stable habit of the writer, not a property of which route through the problem was chosen: R13, R21, R34 and R47 are all maximally compressed yet sit on opposite sides of the disagreement slice from equally-compressed R05 and R30, so the trait tracks the writer rather than the route. Tagged mixed because a practised regular may also be more likely to reach for the standard route.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's accumulated practice in this format (prolific regular vs first-time poster)

proposals.name: Chat-register typography, interjections, emoticons
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT of informal chat typography in the post: sentence-initial lowercase 'i', dropped apostrophes and contractions ('didnt', 'im', 'u', 'cuz', 'ngl', 'fr'), interjections and exclamations ('Bro', 'Um no', 'Holy cow', 'Dangit', 'bleh', 'ok, so first'), stretched vowels or letter runs ('nooooo', 'hmmm'), forum emoticon codes and smilies (:D, :-D, :o, :(, :yoda:), and trailing sign-offs like 'rip', 'Cheers'. Count occurrence density across the post, not just presence. 0 = uniformly formal written prose with no such markers; 10 = the post reads as chat throughout.
