Score only the EXTENT of these typographic markers. You must NOT judge whether informality is appropriate, whether the poster seems serious, or whether the mathematics is any good.
proposals.rationale: R10 is almost entirely chat typography ('Bro', 'i didnt have courage', 'rip me fr'); R15 ends on 'and nooooo' with a ':('; R54 opens 'Um no' with ':o'; R38 opens 'Holy cow this configuration is so nice :-D'; R07 closes on ':yoda:'; R56 self-labels 'Scuffed troll solution'. These markers are orthographic habit and mood at the keyboard, visible in both halves of the slice (R09 and R56 on one side, R10/R15/R35/R54 on the other), so they cannot be a reading of which route the post takes.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Named collaborators and credit lines
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the post attributes its content to people other than the sole author: an explicit 'Solved with <name>' or 'joint with' line, bolded or tagged usernames, thanks or acknowledgements directed at named individuals, or first-person plural that is clearly a group rather than an expository 'we' (e.g. naming who found which step). 0 = no person other than the author is named or credited anywhere; 10 = the post is framed throughout as the output of a named group, with several individuals identified. Score only how much explicit co-attribution is present. You must NOT judge whether collaboration is legitimate, whether the credit is deserved, or whether the solution is better for it.
proposals.rationale: R07 opens 'Solved with S.Ragnork1729, SilverBlaze_SY and HACK_IN_MATHS' in bold; R50 opens 'Solved with mathapple101'; R17 opens '@above thanks!'. Nothing about a credit line is a statement about the route taken, yet it is a visible, easily-learned token that co-occurs with a whole cluster of writer types. Tagged mixed because a group that works a problem together may genuinely converge on the most standard attack.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's social embedding on the forum (study group, mutuals, following) — an unseen factor whose only textual trace is the credit line

proposals.name: Contest-conditions self-report and score talk
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the post narrates the circumstances of its own production under exam conditions: phrases such as 'my solution during the contest', 'in-contest', 'I wrote this on the test', reported grades or points ('somehow got a 7/7', 'hoping it's not more than 1 point off', 'I sure do hope it is valid'), reported elapsed time ('it took ~1.3 hours'), or comparisons to other problems on the same paper ('meanwhile I thought #4 was far harder'). 0 = the post says nothing about when or under what conditions it was written; 10 = several such self-reports, and the framing of the whole post is 'here is what I did on the day'. Score only how much such self-report is present. You must NOT judge whether the claim is credible or whether writing under contest conditions makes the post better or worse.
proposals.rationale: R26 hides its body under 'My solution during the contest (different from the others)'; R60 opens 'Here is my solution during the contest, with bit modifications'; R58 opens 'Here is my cursed solution which somehow got a 7/7'; R28 reports '~1.3 hours' and 'I sure do hope it is valid'; R49 worries 'I'm hoping its not more than 1 point off'. This is a timing fingerprint: it says when the text was produced, not what route it takes. Tagged mixed because a contestant writing on the day has not yet read anyone else's approach, which can genuinely shift which route appears.
proposals.upstream_parent: timing of production/submission relative to the competition (a same-week contestant post versus a later archival write-up)

proposals.name: Self-directed doubt, abandonment and non-completion talk
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the post talks about the author's own difficulty, doubt, confusion or failure to finish: self-deprecation ('maybe I am just dumb', 'cuz im dumb', 'I was scared'), reported abandonment or stopping ('I started doubting myself and I stopped'), open questions addressed to readers ('Does this work?', 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?', 'Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?', 'I'm getting 391'), self-labelling of the work as cheap, scuffed, cursed, oversimplified, a fakesolve, a sketch, or storage. 0 = the post asserts its content flatly with no commentary on the author's state; 10 = doubt, confusion or self-deprecation is a running thread of the post. Score only how much of this talk is present. You must NOT judge whether the doubt is warranted, whether the argument is actually complete, or whether the self-labelling is accurate.
proposals.rationale: R02 is a question post ('I am confused on the wiki solution #2 ... Wouldn't that be overcounting?'); R45 ends 'Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?'; R15 reports stopping halfway; R09 opens 'Dangit this felt surprisingly hard or maybe I am just dumb'; R42 hides under 'fakesolve'; R56 says 'Scuffed troll solution'; R35 hides under 'sketch'. The trait is a register of self-presentation and it appears on both sides of the slice (R02/R09/R45/R56 versus R10/R15/R35/R28), so it is a writer-state fingerprint, not a route signal. Tagged mixed because a post that openly stops partway genuinely contains less of any route at all.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's seniority/confidence in the format, and their expectation of being answered by the thread

proposals.name: Assistance-polished sectioned exposition with strategy headers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the post is laid out as a polished, pre-planned document rather than a running write-up: numbered or titled top-level sections ('1. The Pigeonhole Strategy', '2. Constructing the Triplet', 'Conclusion'), coloured or bolded section headers, an explicit statement of the plan before executing it, formal discourse connectives ('It suffices to', 'Let us construct', 'We now prove that', 'Substituting our expressions', 'This implies that'), symmetric restatement of what was just derived, and a closing summary paragraph that repeats the result. 0 = no sectioning, no plan announcement, the argument simply runs; 10 = fully sectioned with headers, an announced plan, uniform textbook connectives and a summarising conclusion. Score only the amount of this document scaffolding. You must NOT judge whether the write-up is clear, correct, or whether polish indicates outside help.
proposals.rationale: R37 has four coloured numbered section headers plus a 'Conclusion' block and uniformly formal connectives; R33 and R51 carry heavily formatted Lemma/Claim scaffolding with restated conclusions; R58 lays out labelled Cases and Subcases exhaustively. Against these, R30 and R39 run as unbroken streams of substitutions. Layout polish is applied after the mathematical route has been chosen, so it is downstream of presentation rather than of route. Tagged mixed because the same care that produces sectioning may also push an author toward the most canonical presentation of an argument.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing or drafting assistance (rewriting, templating, or an assistant) applied before posting

proposals.name: Thread-position deixis: presupposes earlier posts exist
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the post's language presupposes that other posts already exist above it in the same thread: direct address to a previous poster ('@above', 'I think his monovariant is', 'I already addressed this in my previous post'), positioning relative to unnamed others ('similar to above', 'different from the others', 'A different solution for those who understand less about', 'Not recognizing the root of unity, I came up with'), quoting or arguing with material attributed to elsewhere on the site ('the wiki solution #2'), edit markers and afterthoughts ('Edit:', 'Added Later:', 'Edit: The previous result can also be shown'), and thread-management remarks ('This should be moved to High School Intermediate'). Judge ONLY the deictic language visible in this post; you have no access to any other post and must not attempt to guess what was said above. 0 = the post engages the bare problem as though nothing had been posted yet; 10 = the post is unintelligible except as a reply, threaded throughout with references to prior posts. You must NOT judge whether replying is appropriate or whether the post adds anything.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3 channel. R17 opens '@above thanks!' and labels itself 'p9:'; R59 opens '@above that is listing everything out'; R54 opens 'Um no, I already addressed this in my previous post'; R09 says 'here's my solution similar to above'; R02 argues with 'the wiki solution #2'; R26 hides under '(different from the others)'; R38 carries 'Edit:' and 'Added Later:' bullets; R40 ends with a forum-move request. A post cannot carry these markers unless it is late in the order, so the channel reads arrival position off the text; arrival position is not the route the post takes.
proposals.upstream_parent: position of this post in the thread's arrival order

proposals.name: Era-marked markup, notation and link style
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the post carries typographic markers that date it to an older period of the forum's markup: legacy auto-converted operators written as macros (\equal{}, \minus{}, \plus{}), stray spaces inside inline math after the opening dollar ('$ 4$', '$ x^3 \minus{} xyz$'), deprecated LaTeX environments (eqnarray, \atop, \overwithdelims), bare http:// URLs in [url=...] tags, and older sub/superscript-padding artefacts such as trailing empty braces on variables (n_{}^{}, S_n^{}, n^{}_{}). 0 = none of these appear; the post uses current inline/display conventions throughout; 10 = several distinct legacy markers, and the post's markup is legacy throughout. Score only the presence and density of these markers. You must NOT judge whether the notation is clean or whether an older style is worse.
proposals.rationale: MODE 3 channel with a purely orthographic readout. R18 uses '\equal{}' and a bare en.wikipedia.org [url=...] link; R54 uses both '\minus{}' and '\equal{}'; R32 shows the legacy spacing '$ 4$' and '$ 31$'; R52 uses eqnarray and \atop; R21's problem statement carries the n_{}^{} padding artefact. These markers time-stamp the writing and nothing else; a 2008 post and a 2024 post can take exactly the same route, so any association is a dating artefact.
proposals.upstream_parent: the calendar era in which the post was written, i.e. how long after the thread opened it arrived

proposals.name: Forum markup furniture: hide blocks, colour-tagged claims, boxed answers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the post uses the forum's own markup furniture: [hide]/[hide=...] spoiler blocks wrapping some or all of the body (and how much of the body they wrap), [color=...] tags applied to structural words such as Claim, Lemma, Proof, or to a highlighted final inequality, [b]/[i] tags used as structural labels rather than emphasis, [list] blocks, tabular environments, \boxed{} or \blacksquare/\square terminators, and named hide-block captions ('Solution', 'Casework', 'what I did', 'sketch'). 0 = plain text and plain LaTeX with none of this furniture; 10 = the post is heavily furnished, with spoiler wrapping, coloured structural labels and boxed terminators throughout. Score only the amount of markup furniture. You must NOT judge whether the formatting aids the reader or whether hiding the solution is courteous.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4 channel on the named 'typographic and markup habit' prior. R03, R16, R22, R27, R29 and R51 all wrap Claim/Proof in [color=#f00]/[color=#00f] bold tags; R01, R26, R32, R33, R35, R36, R40, R45, R48 and R53 wrap their bodies in [hide] blocks with captions; R01, R21, R34, R41 and R55 terminate in \boxed{} plus \blacksquare. The furniture is a keyboard habit that travels with the author across problems, and the slice shows it on both sides (R01/R26/R33/R36/R45 versus R03/R16/R27/R35/R53), so it indexes the writer, not the route.
proposals.upstream_parent: the poster's habitual markup practice, itself a function of how long they have been posting in this format

proposals.name: Multiple-choice answer-extraction framing in the post
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the EXTENT to which the post is written as the extraction of one lettered option rather than as a free-standing argument: it names or boxes an answer letter (\boxed{\textbf{(C)}}, 'Choice (E) is obviously false', 'so the answer must be (C) 36'), it reasons over the option list itself ('the only answer choice that is odd and 1 mod 3', 'the answer choices are all clearly distinct', 'the choices are furthermore all real'), it appeals to the answer being one of five, or it plugs candidate options back in. Also count lighter traces: a final numeric value asserted with no proof obligation, or an explicit remark that the shortcut suffices because only the option must be identified. 0 = the post never behaves as though a fixed option list exists and argues to an unconditioned conclusion; 10 = the option list is the organising device of the whole post. Score only how much option-directed framing is present. You must NOT judge whether shortcutting to the letter is legitimate or whether the reasoning is sound.
proposals.rationale: MODE 4 channel on the named 'kind of problem' prior. R01 selects by elimination ('the only answer choice that is odd and 1 mod 3'); R23 concludes 'Choice (E) is obviously false' without touching the other four; R36 explicitly reasons 'the answer choices are all clearly distinct and extant over F_25, so it suffices to compute over said field'; R08 and R14 end on a bare letter. Against these, R03, R28, R33, R42 and R51 are proof-obligation posts with no letters anywhere. The option-list framing is a property of the venue the thread sits in and of the crowd it draws, and it is measurable in the post itself. Tagged mixed because on a five-option item the space of sensible routes is genuinely narrower, so the same upstream factor can also move route-agreement.
proposals.upstream_parent: the kind of problem the thread hangs off (short computational contest item versus open-ended olympiad problem), which sets the population of posters and their norms

proposals.name: Invariant-driving substitutions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when carefully chosen substitutions produce strong identities that directly constrain the unknown and are chained into the proof; score 0 when substitutions are mostly ad hoc and yield no reusable constraint.
proposals.rationale: R02, R14, and R44 derive several decisive identities from paired substitutions before classifying the functions.

proposals.name: Global branch consistency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post first identifies pointwise alternatives and then rigorously proves that only one alternative can hold globally; score 0 when it accepts pointwise choices without ruling out mixtures.
proposals.rationale: R08, R30, and R49 explicitly confront the possibility that different inputs take different pointwise forms.

proposals.name: Auxiliary structure encoding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post defines a graph, transformed function, or other auxiliary structure whose properties exactly encode the original condition; score 0 when it remains in the original notation without a structurally useful reformulation.
proposals.rationale: R01 introduces a shifted function, R12 converts the problem to an odd-cycle graph, and R51 defines good-prime relations.

proposals.name: Complete parameter coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a parameterized construction is accompanied by a proof that its valid parameter ranges cover every permitted instance; score 0 when it supplies only examples or asserts coverage without closing the gaps.
proposals.rationale: R36, R47, and R56 construct triples and explicitly address coverage of all n at least 100.

proposals.name: Equality-case propagation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an inequality is used with its exact equality condition and that condition is translated into the requested ratios, lengths, or integers; score 0 when the inequality is cited only as a bound.
proposals.rationale: R05 extracts side ratios from Cauchy equality, while R31 and R54 use equality-sensitive inequalities to connect local bounds to the target.

proposals.name: Exact modular periodicity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post proves a valid period or residue restriction and then uses it exhaustively to constrain the target; score 0 when it merely reports a pattern or invokes a modulus without justifying all relevant cases.
proposals.rationale: R10 uses parity and modulo 3 cycles, R17 uses root-of-unity periodicity, and R40 combines congruences to exclude all larger cases.

proposals.name: Bijective counting control
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post gives an exhaustive, non-overcounting encoding or involution for the counted objects and handles ordering or duplicate cases; score 0 when it lists cases incompletely or counts without controlling overlap.
proposals.rationale: R07 counts congruent pairs across all parameters, R18 counts circular arrangements, and R41 assigns each element to a unique transition category.

proposals.name: Geometric incidence chain
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when auxiliary lines, circles, or points create a clearly justified chain of cyclicity, similarity, parallelism, or radical-axis relations leading to the target; score 0 when it gives isolated angle observations without a connecting chain.
proposals.rationale: R04, R15, and R23 use multiple linked geometric incidences to reach concurrency or length identities.

proposals.name: Exact optimization reduction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the variable objective is rewritten as a fixed product, distance, norm, or other simpler quantity, and the extremal bound is shown attainable; score 0 when an extremal estimate or guess is stated without this reduction.
proposals.rationale: R27 reduces the complex expression to a distance bound, while R46 reduces the area problem to minimizing a single geometric distance.

proposals.name: Representation-preserving identity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a factorization, recurrence, or scaling identity transforms the original quantity into the exact representation being counted or constructed, with indices and multiplicities checked; score 0 when a suggestive identity is left disconnected from the requested quantity.
proposals.rationale: R25 factors the power quotient into disjoint term blocks, R33 uses scaling to preserve both equations, and R22 identifies a Fibonacci ratio identity.

proposals.name: Finite-process mechanism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post explains why arbitrary allowed moves create a descending potential or a terminal symmetric configuration, including ties and degeneracies; score 0 when eventual termination is only asserted.
proposals.rationale: R26 discusses a potential for repeated subtraction operations, and R60 explicitly handles every type of initial move before reaching paired values.

proposals.name: Construction admissibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a constructed object is checked to be integral, distinct, ordered, and within every stated domain restriction, as well as satisfying the defining relations; score 0 when formulas are presented without these checks.
proposals.rationale: R03 checks prime-factor and size restrictions, while R56 and R57 verify that constructed triples lie in the card interval and have the required pairwise sums.

proposals.name: Necessity and sufficiency closure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post both excludes every remaining case and verifies that each retained form satisfies the original conditions; score 0 when it gives only a candidate, only a contradiction, or an unverified final assertion.
proposals.rationale: R02, R40, and R50 each illustrate the importance of combining exclusion arguments with explicit verification of the surviving possibilities.

proposals.name: Duality-based cancellation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a reciprocal, inverse, conjugate, reflection, or other visible duality is identified and used to force cancellation or equality; score 0 when the paired structure is ignored in favor of unrelated expansion.
proposals.rationale: R01 uses reciprocal inputs, R17 pairs powers with inverses, and R39 exploits unit-circle conjugacy and symmetry.

proposals.name: Bridge validation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every non-obvious theorem invocation, equality, sign claim, and arithmetic bridge is checked against the stated hypotheses and target; score 0 when the proof relies on an unsupported shortcut or an unverified imported claim.
proposals.rationale: R06 invokes the hook-length formula without setup, R16 equates unequal quantities heuristically, and R28 and R38 make major conclusions without validating the intervening claims.

proposals.name: Emotional enthusiasm
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of overt excitement, praise, emojis, or exclamatory reaction; do not judge whether the reaction is deserved or whether the solution is good.

proposals.name: Self-doubt commentary
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of apologies, uncertainty, embarrassment, self-criticism, or retrospective doubt; do not judge the underlying work.

proposals.name: Legacy forum markup
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of platform-specific legacy tags, color codes, hide blocks, list syntax, or HTML-like markup; do not judge whether the formatting is good.

proposals.name: Derivation compression
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent to which intermediate steps are omitted in favor of terse assertions, formulas, or a final calculation; do not judge correctness or elegance.
proposals.rationale: Experienced forum writers may habitually compress routine exposition, and that practice may also correlate with route choice, so this is a mixed nuisance. Compression is visible in R20, R29, and R45.

proposals.name: Peer-directed address
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of direct replies, at-mentions, second-person language, or wording aimed at people currently in the thread; do not judge the mathematical content.
proposals.rationale: Writing to active peers can change register and framing without determining the solution approach. Examples include R29, R34, R36, and R51.

proposals.name: Collaboration attribution
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of explicit references to collaborators, helpers, prior assistance, or thanking another participant; do not judge the value of that assistance.
proposals.rationale: Collaboration leaves visible attribution traces and may also influence which route the author adopts, making this mixed. Examples include R16, R34, and R53.
proposals.upstream_parent: collaboration and social assistance

proposals.name: Thread-position cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of language presupposing earlier or later thread entries, such as edits, previous posts, alternative solutions, or references to a wiki; do not judge the solution itself.
proposals.rationale: A post's unseen position can leave chronological cues, and exposure to earlier entries could also affect the adopted route. Such cues occur in R09, R15, R26, and R36.

proposals.name: Display-layout habit
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of display-equation blocks, aligned derivations, named claims, boxed conclusions, or highly segmented mathematical layout; do not judge whether the layout is clear or correct.
proposals.rationale: Personal formatting habits can be predictive of model behavior without being evidence about the reference approach. The pattern varies across R05, R17, R41, and R49.
