proposals.name: Answer-choice anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of explicit option letters, answer-choice elimination, contest-answer formatting, or correction of a numerical choice; do not judge whether the selected answer is right.
proposals.rationale: Multiple-choice framing creates salient lexical and numerical cues unrelated to approach matching. Examples include R03, R29, R43, R45, and R47.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Timing provenance
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the extent of explicit claims about contest timing, time spent, being a first attempt, later revision, or when the solution was produced; do not judge the author's performance.
proposals.rationale: Timing and revision leave textual provenance markers and can also affect which approach was available or chosen, so this is mixed. Examples include R14, R26, R36, and R51.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing and revision process

proposals.name: Reusable governing identity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post derives a compact relation and reuses it for several decisive deductions; score 0 when it consists only of isolated manipulations with no reusable relation.
proposals.rationale: Rows R02 and R12 repeatedly derive identities such as f(f(x))=x^2f(x) and use them to organize the proof. This distinguishes structural reasoning from a sequence of locally plausible substitutions.

proposals.name: Strategic specialization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when substitutions are clearly chosen because they expose the equation's decisive structure and their consequences are explained; score 0 when substitutions are arbitrary, unexplained, or do not advance the target.
proposals.rationale: Rows R12 and R34 use carefully selected inputs such as (x,0), (x,x^2/2), and (x,y^2) to expose the functional equation's structure. This captures whether special cases are strategically informative rather than merely numerous.

proposals.name: Global closure of local alternatives
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when pointwise possibilities are shown to combine into one globally consistent form, with mixed assignments explicitly ruled out; score 0 when the post stops after listing possibilities for each individual input.
proposals.rationale: Rows R16 and R25 first obtain the pointwise alternatives 0, x^2, and -x^2, then address the essential mixed-pattern obstruction. This is evidence of solving the global problem rather than only deriving local constraints.

proposals.name: Operational use of symmetry
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a nontrivial symmetry or involution is identified and then used to equate expressions, reduce cases, or construct the conclusion; score 0 when symmetry is merely mentioned or has no proof-driving role.
proposals.rationale: Rows R02 and R17 use evenness and substitutions involving x and -x to collapse the functional equation. The criterion captures whether symmetry is an active solution mechanism.

proposals.name: Witness plus full coverage
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post gives an explicit witness family and proves that its parameter ranges cover every allowed input, including boundary gaps; score 0 when it gives only an isolated example or leaves coverage unproved.
proposals.rationale: Rows R22 and R39 construct triples and prove their intervals cover all n in the required range. This separates a genuinely general construction from an attractive but incomplete witness.

proposals.name: State invariant or monovariant
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post identifies a quantity or state relation preserved or decreasing under every move, handles ties or exceptional transitions, and explains termination; score 0 when it merely names a monovariant without proving those properties.
proposals.rationale: Row R01 highlights that a proposed difference may require multiple steps to decrease, while R55 discusses tracking inversion changes through successive card moves. These motivate explicit transition-level reasoning for dynamic problems.

proposals.name: Independent-choice encoding
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when each object is assigned to an independent slot or state and the correspondence is shown to be bijective, yielding the count; score 0 when a product or sum is asserted without explaining what its terms represent.
proposals.rationale: Rows R06 and R52 encode subset growth and binary expansions through independent placement choices and products. The criterion detects whether a compact count faithfully represents the original objects.

proposals.name: Equality-case extraction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an inequality is accompanied by a precise equality characterization and that equality condition is translated into the requested structure; score 0 when the inequality only supplies a bound with no equality analysis.
proposals.rationale: Rows R15 and R48 invoke convexity or Cauchy-Schwarz, but the useful solution requires understanding when equality occurs. This criterion captures the structural information carried by the sharp bound.

proposals.name: Complete modular filter
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when congruences, parity, or periodicity are selected to eliminate all alternatives and the relevant residue cases are checked completely; score 0 when the post gives only an isolated congruence observation or unsupported residue conclusion.
proposals.rationale: Rows R41, R47, and R49 use parity and modular residues to narrow the answer to a unique possibility. The criterion distinguishes a complete arithmetic obstruction from decorative modular arithmetic.

proposals.name: Exhaustive case partition
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when cases are disjoint, exhaustive, include degenerate or boundary cases, and each branch reaches a conclusion; score 0 when cases are ad hoc, overlapping, or leave a possible branch untreated.
proposals.rationale: Rows R04 and R50 organize their arguments around mutually exclusive possibilities such as zero values, prime cases, and sign patterns. This helps distinguish a controlled proof architecture from informal case listing.

proposals.name: Factorization with arithmetic forcing
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when factorization or divisibility turns the equations into bounded integer factors and then exploits primality, parity, or gcd constraints; score 0 when equations remain expanded without any forced-factor argument.
proposals.rationale: Rows R50 and R57 derive products such as p(q-1)=(y-x)(y+x) and use primality to force a factor. This is a visible signal of arithmetic structure rather than numerical trial.

proposals.name: Recurrence-driven derivation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post defines the correct recurrence or decomposition, establishes initial conditions, and derives the target pattern by induction or an equivalent systematic argument; score 0 when it merely guesses a pattern from a few computed values.
proposals.rationale: Rows R26 and R54 derive the recurrence for ordered powers-of-two representations and prove the oddness pattern. The criterion captures disciplined use of recursive structure.

proposals.name: Geometric incidence chain
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when named geometric relations form a connected dependency chain—such as parallelism, cyclicity, similarity, or radical axes—that ends at the requested incidence or length; score 0 when claims are disconnected, diagram-based, or unsupported.
proposals.rationale: Rows R09 and R40 build several linked cyclicity, parallelism, similarity, and radical-axis claims. This identifies whether a geometry post has a coherent structural route to its conclusion.

proposals.name: Objective-preserving optimization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the varying target is rigorously reduced to a simpler quantity using a fixed or monotone factor, and the optimization direction is preserved; score 0 when calculations are performed without establishing that they optimize the requested quantity.
proposals.rationale: Row R23 reduces the area minimization to minimizing AX, while R45 reduces an integer condition to a sharp Minkowski bound. This captures whether the optimization target is structurally controlled.

proposals.name: Statement and legality fidelity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post respects the exact statement and checks domain, signs, distinctness, ordering, integrality, and endpoint conditions wherever needed; score 0 when it silently changes the problem or accepts invalid algebra or geometry.
proposals.rationale: Rows R10, R21, and R31 illustrate how an apparently concise argument can rely on an invalid right-angle construction, an unjustified equality, or a misread calendar condition. This criterion identifies reasoning that is genuinely tied to the stated problem.

proposals.name: Thread-position cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post explicitly presupposes or references other entries in the thread, such as earlier solutions, numbered solutions, or replies; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: Posts such as R02, R17, and R38 contain visible references to previous discussion or wiki ordering. Thread position can leave this trace and can also affect which approach an author chooses, but the trace itself is not a quality judgment.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Future-reader orientation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post addresses a broad future audience through standalone exposition, explanatory framing, or reader-oriented labels; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R33 use reader-facing exposition and labels, unlike the conversational stance in R20 or R57. Audience orientation is socially upstream and may influence wording independently of solution quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: poster’s intended audience

proposals.name: Collaboration provenance
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text visibly attributes the work to collaborators, commenters, handles, or joint solving; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: R28 names several collaborators, R42 says it was solved with another user, and R17 addresses someone above. Collaboration can affect which ideas appear, while attribution markers are nuisance signals visible to a text-only model.
proposals.upstream_parent: assistance and social collaboration

proposals.name: Insider forum register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post uses compressed insider conventions, unexplained shorthand, routine assertion labels, or dense expert-to-expert prose; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: R22, R40, and R46 use highly compressed forum-native notation and abbreviated proof structure. A practiced regular may leave this fingerprint, which is distinct from the mathematical content and can also correlate with route selection.
proposals.upstream_parent: author’s standing and practice in the forum format

proposals.name: Revision-state traces
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post contains visible signs of drafting, editing, abandoned attempts, uncertainty, corrections, or post-contest revision; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: R13 reports stopping after an abandoned calculation, R20 describes a long tentative proof, and R26 includes an explicit correction. Such process traces can predict text reception without themselves expressing mathematical quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing history and production process

proposals.name: Era-marked notation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post displays historically or platform-specific notation such as legacy hide tags, color tags, Asymptote, custom macros, or older forum syntax; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: R04, R21, R23, and R30 show distinctive legacy markup or rendering conventions. These are traces of platform history rather than evidence about the mathematical route.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission era and forum software conventions

proposals.name: Affective self-presentation
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post uses slang, emojis, exclamations, apology, self-deprecation, excitement, or other emotional stance markers; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: R07 says the problem should be moved, R13 uses an emoticon and self-doubt, and R21 or R57 use exuberant informal language. These interpersonal signals can be predictive of model behavior while being unrelated to solution quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: social self-presentation and audience effects

proposals.name: Quick-answer template
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post follows a short contest-answer template: immediate answer choice or number, one local calculation, and little proof architecture; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: R10, R12, R17, and R50 present compact answer-choice solutions with minimal setup. The genre of the attached problem can produce this textual form, which may correlate with route choice but is not itself a quality judgment.
proposals.upstream_parent: kind of problem and its competition ecology

proposals.name: Markup scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post uses visual organization such as hides, colored headings, bullets, boxed answers, quote blocks, or elaborate sectioning; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: R04 uses colored claims, R23 uses multiple colored sections, and R29 uses hidden blocks and lemma headings. The amount of forum presentation scaffolding is a formatting nuisance independent of mathematical merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: poster’s typographic and markup habits

proposals.name: Tangential digression
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post extends beyond the stated problem with generalizations, alternate observations, convergence discussion, unrelated commentary, or meta-reflection; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: R09 develops a broader polygon and convergence discussion, R20 adds meta-reflection, and R54 includes an unrelated reference to another problem. Such excess material is visibly predictive but need not indicate anything about the intended solution approach.
proposals.upstream_parent: author’s available time and self-presentation goals

proposals.name: Problem-specific structural reduction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post derives a compact invariant, normal form, or structural reformulation tailored to the problem; score 0 when it only performs isolated substitutions or calculations without exposing structure.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R31 build strong problem-specific reductions, whereas R12 and R37 mainly report a short computation or observation.

proposals.name: Chained intermediate claims
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when several clearly stated lemmas or claims form a logically connected chain from the setup to the conclusion; score 0 when observations remain disconnected or the final result appears abruptly.
proposals.rationale: R09 and R41 organize long geometry arguments through dependent claims, unlike the disconnected reasoning in R07 and R25.

proposals.name: Global coverage of cases
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the argument explicitly covers every permitted parameter range, branch, parity, or exceptional case; score 0 when it handles only a convenient subcase or a single example.
proposals.rationale: R34 and R60 cover all n through intervals and parity cases, while R15 and R37 rely on one narrowly chosen situation.

proposals.name: Fully verified constructive witness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an explicit construction is given and every required property, bound, distinctness condition, and relation is checked; score 0 when a proposed witness is merely asserted or only partly checked.
proposals.rationale: R04 and R34 verify constructed numbers against several constraints, while R01 and R58 leave important construction or arithmetic claims unjustified.

proposals.name: Completeness of candidate classification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post both derives all possible candidates and directly verifies that each candidate satisfies the original conditions; score 0 when it guesses candidates, verifies only some, or never excludes alternatives.
proposals.rationale: R02 and R42 classify and check all functional-equation solutions, whereas R28 and R25 give conclusions with little candidate analysis.

proposals.name: Global consistency beyond pointwise options
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post recognizes that local alternatives must be made globally consistent and proves that mixed choices cannot occur; score 0 when it treats independent pointwise possibilities as if they automatically defined one valid object.
proposals.rationale: R17 and R33 explicitly resolve the pointwise trap, while R49 begins such an analysis but leaves its global argument incomplete.

proposals.name: Strategic use of symmetry
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when symmetry, invariance, or an interchangeable reformulation materially reduces the argument and is used correctly; score 0 when symmetry is absent, accidental, or merely mentioned without consequence.
proposals.rationale: R23 exploits circular ordering and R40 exploits cyclic equality conditions, while R26 and R58 use geometric or algebraic observations without a sound symmetry-based reduction.

proposals.name: Legality and boundary control
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when domain restrictions, positivity, nonzero denominators, ordering, integrality, and endpoint conditions are tracked whenever they matter; score 0 when such conditions are ignored or silently assumed.
proposals.rationale: R16 and R20 carefully control primality, divisibility, and modular denominators, while R07 and R45 omit important feasibility checks.

proposals.name: Exact target-directed algebra
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when algebraic transformations are chosen to expose the requested quantity or a decisive factorization, with equality conditions visible; score 0 when manipulation is indirect, approximate, or unrelated to the target.
proposals.rationale: R19 and R22 turn the target into decisive factorizations or termwise inequalities, unlike the heuristic algebra in R58 and R21.

proposals.name: Transparent combinatorial bookkeeping
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when objects, cases, multiplicities, and overcounting are explicitly defined and counted; score 0 when a formula or named principle replaces the actual bookkeeping.
proposals.rationale: R13 and R23 explain what is being counted and why, whereas R28 and R59 give compressed counts with little underlying enumeration.

proposals.name: Hypothesis-aware theorem use
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every invoked theorem or principle has its hypotheses checked and its conclusion translated into the needed statement; score 0 when a theorem is only name-dropped or applied without justification.
proposals.rationale: R40 derives the equality conditions behind Cauchy-Schwarz and R41 explains radical-axis applications, while R57 and R59 invoke powerful formulas with minimal justification.

proposals.name: Notation and equation consistency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when symbols, indices, signs, substitutions, and displayed equations remain consistent throughout; score 0 when notation changes, equations contain unexplained typos, or later steps do not follow from earlier ones.
proposals.rationale: R06 and R18 maintain a coherent sequence of functional identities, while R10 and R22 contain visible notation or formula inconsistencies.

proposals.name: Useful abstraction of repetition
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the post replaces repetitive work with a justified recurrence, graph, generating principle, or algebraic encoding that is then used effectively; score 0 when it either blindly enumerates or introduces abstraction without payoff.
proposals.rationale: R04 and R43 use graph or recurrence abstractions to control many cases, whereas R12 and R28 largely rely on direct enumeration.

proposals.name: Relevant and economical machinery
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when every substantial technique directly advances the proof and the argument avoids distracting generalizations or tangents; score 0 when most of the post is irrelevant, ornamental, or meta-commentary.
proposals.rationale: R41 and R31 keep sophisticated machinery tied to the target, while R03 and R11 include extensive detours beyond what their immediate conclusions require.

proposals.name: Locally justified transitions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when each nontrivial inference is supported by an equation, construction, or stated reason that an independent reader can check; score 0 when key steps are asserted with phrases such as “obvious,” “clearly,” or “it follows” without support.
proposals.rationale: R18 and R42 make their crucial transitions checkable, whereas R07 and R25 leave central inferences as unsupported assertions.

proposals.name: Thread-history residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post presupposes thread history through references to earlier posts, numbered solutions, edits, later additions, or alternative posts. Judge only visible wording; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: R08 refers to a previous post, while R12 addresses an earlier contributor and R27 discusses a wiki solution. Such traces reveal where the post entered the thread and can affect reception without describing the mathematical route.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream / submission timing

proposals.name: Social-graph cues
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of visible social-network residue, including usernames, @-replies, collaboration credits, thanks, or comments about other contributors. Judge only visible text; do not judge whether this feature is good.
proposals.rationale: R08 addresses another poster directly, R22 credits three collaborators, and R43 begins with a reply to someone above. These cues expose social position and interaction patterns that may affect reception independently of the solution method.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's forum standing, following, and collaboration network

proposals.name: Audience-address mode
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post is framed as immediate conversation versus a self-contained write-up for later readers, using greetings, replies, reader-directed asides, or archival exposition. Judge only this address mode; do not judge whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: R18 uses conversational slang and self-address, whereas R11 and R38 use a more archival lemma-and-proof presentation. Audience orientation leaves a textual trace that can influence reception separately from mathematical content.
proposals.upstream_parent: intended audience and reading context

proposals.name: Forum-era residue
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the amount of period-specific forum syntax, typography, orthography, or notation, such as legacy BBCode, obsolete tags, escaped operators, or era-marked slang. Judge only the visible residue; do not judge whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: R05 uses colored BBCode and legacy formatting, R10 contains unusual escaped operators, and R35 includes an old-style external URL tag. These traces can identify when and under which interface the post was produced without stating its route.
proposals.upstream_parent: posting era and forum software conventions

proposals.name: Markup fluency
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of deliberate forum-format conventions such as hide blocks, colored headings, claim/proof labels, list tags, display structure, or boxed conclusions. Judge only formatting presence; do not judge whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: R05 uses repeated colored claims and proof labels, R23 uses numerous colored claims, and R38 uses tagged lists and claims. Formatting fluency can signal practiced participation and affect reception without being a mathematical criterion.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice and fluency in the forum format

proposals.name: Self-talk and hedging
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the amount of explicit self-commentary about confidence, confusion, fear, embarrassment, uncertainty, effort, or perceived mistakes. Judge only the amount of self-talk; do not judge whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: R09 mentions realizing an omission and worrying about lost points, R18 includes fear, embarrassment, and self-deprecation, and R48 describes stopping after doubt. These emotional traces may affect reception while not measuring the mathematical approach.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's confidence, contest stress, and revision state

proposals.name: Specialist-name density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of named specialist tools, theorems, external references, or advanced formal frameworks appearing in the prose. Judge only their visible presence; do not judge whether their use is good or correct.
proposals.rationale: R17 names Miquel's Theorem, radical axes, and symmedians; R35 cites the hook-length formula externally; R56 invokes finite fields. Such pedigree markers can influence reception independently of the underlying route.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's training, seniority, and exposition habits

proposals.name: Answer-choice anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the post foregrounds answer choices, option letters, boxed numerical outputs, or answer-checking language. Judge only this assessment-format trace; do not judge whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: R12 explicitly corrects an answer choice, R33 identifies choice C, and R46 dismisses choice E. These visible test-taking conventions can affect reception without indicating the substantive solution approach.
proposals.upstream_parent: assessment format and answer-checking practice

proposals.name: Compression profile
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of extreme terseness, omitted intermediate steps, fragmentary prose, or unusually expansive step-by-step exposition. Judge only amount and compression of text; do not judge whether it is good.
proposals.rationale: R08 is nearly a fragmentary reply, R18 is highly compressed and conversational, while R10 and R11 provide long derivations. Length and step density can predict textual treatment without encoding a quality judgment.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Difficulty/venue labeling
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the post explicitly labels the problem as easy, hard, routine, contest-specific, school-level, or otherwise places it in a venue or difficulty category. Judge only the presence of such labels; do not judge whether they are good.
proposals.rationale: R04 says the problem belongs in a high-school category, R18 discusses a perceived contest difficulty level, and R31 describes a straightforward computational count. Such labels expose problem-context framing that can influence reception without being a solution criterion.
proposals.upstream_parent: kind of problem and perceived venue or difficulty

proposals.name: Assertion notation for systematic substitution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution introduces formal assertion notation (e.g., 'Let P(x,y) denote the assertion') and uses it to label multiple special-value substitutions systematically. Score 0 if no such notation appears and substitutions are unlabeled or ad hoc.
proposals.rationale: Dense_high FE solutions R07, R15, R24, R37, R45, R49, R51, R56, R60 all use P(x,y) notation—a hallmark of the canonical approach the dense model recognizes. Dense_low FE solutions R16 and R26 avoid this notation entirely.

proposals.name: Proportionate mathematical tool selection
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution uses techniques whose sophistication is well-matched to the problem's level. Score 0 if the solution invokes mathematical machinery far more powerful than the problem requires (e.g., finite field theory for a trigonometric identity, representation-theoretic formulas for elementary counting).
proposals.rationale: R08 (dense_low) uses finite fields F_25 for a root-of-unity computation; R09 (dense_low) invokes the hook-length formula for simple 3×3 counting. R04 (dense_high) uses elementary mod-12 arithmetic appropriately. The dense model rewards proportionate tool choice.

proposals.name: Explicit claim-proof structuring
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution contains multiple explicitly labeled claims or lemmas (using 'Claim:', 'Lemma:', or equivalent markers), each with its own proof block. Score 0 if the solution is unstructured flowing prose or raw calculations with no organizational markers.
proposals.rationale: R07, R45, R49, R57, R60 (dense_high) use labeled claim-proof structure. R03, R18, R29 (dense_low) lack such structure. The scorecard may not weight this organizational hallmark heavily enough.

proposals.name: Within-domain problem solving
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution works entirely within the mathematical domain naturally implied by the problem. Score 0 if the solution transfers the problem to a fundamentally different domain (e.g., complex numbers for a real geometry problem, graph theory for a number theory problem).
proposals.rationale: R14 (dense_low) recasts a circle geometry problem on the complex plane; R42 (dense_low) reformulates a number-theory/pigeonhole problem as graph theory. R10, R23, R57 (dense_high) stay within classical geometry.

proposals.name: Quotient-constancy through symmetric comparison
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution derives that a key quotient (e.g., f(x)/x²) is constant across all inputs by comparing two symmetrically-related substitutions (e.g., P(x,y²) vs P(y,x²)). Score 0 if no such ratio-constancy argument appears or constancy is established otherwise.
proposals.rationale: R24, R37, R45, R51 (dense_high) all derive f(x)/x² = constant by comparing P(x,y²) and P(y,x²). R16 and R26 (dense_low) reach the conclusion through entirely different routes, which the dense model does not recognize as canonical.

proposals.name: Named inequality equality case exploitation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution explicitly identifies the equality case of a named inequality (Cauchy-Schwarz, AM-GM, Jensen, Minkowski, etc.) and uses this equality condition to determine the answer. Score 0 if no named inequality equality case is identified or used.
proposals.rationale: R05 (dense_high) identifies the Cauchy-Schwarz equality case to determine side-length ratios. R34 (dense_low) mentions convexity but never completes the argument or identifies the extremal case.

proposals.name: Minimal pigeonhole construction with pairwise properties
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution constructs exactly three objects whose pairwise combinations satisfy a target property (e.g., three numbers whose pairwise sums are all perfect squares) and then invokes the pigeonhole principle on two piles. Score 0 if no such triple construction appears, or if a substantially larger or different structure is used.
proposals.rationale: R35 (dense_high) constructs three numbers with consecutive square pairwise sums and applies pigeonhole. R42 (dense_low) instead constructs a 7-element odd cycle in a graph—a creative but non-canonical approach.

proposals.name: Explicit pointwise-to-global consistency resolution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution explicitly addresses whether an object satisfying conditions pointwise (at each individual input) must take the same form globally, with a clear bridging argument. Score 0 if pointwise information is derived but no global-consistency step appears, or if the issue does not arise.
proposals.rationale: R22, R49, R54, R56, R60 (dense_high) all explicitly resolve the 'pointwise trap'—showing f being 0, x², or −x² at each x individually must be the same choice globally. R37 (dense_high) explicitly notes this trap is avoided. This step is absent from dense_low FE solutions.

proposals.name: Symmetry or evenness as explicit proof milestone
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution proves a symmetry property (e.g., a function is even, a construction is invariant under a swap) as a distinct labeled step that enables subsequent progress. Score 0 if no symmetry property is established and used, or if symmetry is merely assumed.
proposals.rationale: R07, R15, R22, R24, R37, R45, R51, R54 (dense_high) all prove f is even as an explicit milestone before the main ratio argument. Dense_low FE solutions R16, R26 either skip this milestone or derive it through a longer non-standard route.

proposals.name: Overlapping interval coverage for universal quantification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution proves a statement for all parameter values by defining a sequence of intervals and showing they overlap to cover the full range. Score 0 if coverage is handled by exhaustive small-case checking followed by a separate general argument, with no interval-overlap structure.
proposals.rationale: R35 (dense_high) defines intervals I_m = [m²+2m, 2m²−4m] and proves consecutive overlap for m ≥ 9, elegantly covering all n ≥ 100. R06 (dense_low) instead manually checks specific ranges (100–126, 127–144) and then switches to a general construction.

proposals.name: Key identity derivation via natural substitution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution derives a central identity (such as f(f(x)) = x²f(x)) through substitution of an obvious special value (like y = x², y = 0, or y = x²/2) as one of its first major steps. Score 0 if the key identity is derived through a longer chain or different substitution pattern.
proposals.rationale: R07, R15, R22, R24, R37, R45, R49, R51, R54, R56, R60 (dense_high) all derive f(f(x)) = x²f(x) via P(x, x²) or P(x, x²/2) early on. This substitution sequence is the backbone of the canonical approach the dense model detects.

proposals.name: Recurrence identification with modular parity analysis
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution identifies a recurrence relation and then analyzes it modulo small numbers (especially mod 2) to determine which terms have a desired property. Score 0 if no recurrence is identified, or if analysis avoids modular pattern-finding.
proposals.rationale: R32 and R36 (dense_high) both identify the recurrence f(n) = Σf(n−2ᵏ) and analyze mod 2 to conclude f(n) is odd iff n = 2ᵃ−1. R40 (dense_low) uses parity and mod-3 patterns on a simple recursion but for an answer-choice problem in a less canonical way.

proposals.name: Classical circle geometry technique centrality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if, for a problem involving circles, the primary tools are angle chasing, radical axes, power of a point, Miquel's theorem, or cyclic quadrilateral properties. Score 0 if circle geometry is handled primarily through coordinates, complex numbers, or brute trigonometry.
proposals.rationale: R10 (dense_high) uses symmedian chord and angle chasing; R23 (dense_high) uses radical axes and Miquel's theorem; R57 (dense_high) uses angle chasing and radical axes. R14 (dense_low) recasts the entire configuration on the complex plane.

proposals.name: Absence of non-standard auxiliary reformulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution works directly with the given equations or objects without introducing auxiliary functions or non-standard variable substitutions that transform the problem into a different equation. Score 0 if an auxiliary function or substitution is introduced that materially changes the equation's character.
proposals.rationale: R16 and R26 (dense_low) both introduce g(x) = f(x+1), transforming the original FE into a different equation that is then solved via Cauchy-type arguments. Dense_high solutions R24, R37, R45 work directly with f throughout, staying on the canonical path.

proposals.name: Direct proof of problem as stated, without strengthening
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution proves exactly the statement asked without first establishing a materially stronger or generalized result. Score 0 if the solution explicitly or implicitly proves a strengthened version that goes beyond what the problem requires.
proposals.rationale: R19 (dense_low) explicitly states 'We solve this strengthened version of the problem' and proves a more general claim before deducing the required result. R20 (dense_low) introduces auxiliary lemmas about binomial-coefficient optimization. Dense_high solutions like R07, R35, R57 address the problem directly without such detours.

proposals.name: Inter-post referencing and sequence markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text explicitly references other posts, posters, or its place in the thread sequence. Look for phrases such as '@above', 'as above', 'previous post', 'Solution 2', 'different from the others', 'similar to what was posted', or direct replies to a named user. Do not judge whether referencing is good or bad; score only how much such referencing is present.
proposals.rationale: Posts that engage earlier contributions leave conversational markers that make them non-standalone; this is independent of whether their mathematical method matches the canonical write-up. R12 says 'I already addressed this in my previous post'; R21 begins '@above'; R08 says 'similar to above'.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Conversational and emotional register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post uses informal, first-person, or emotionally charged language, including exclamations, self-deprecation, casual interjections (e.g., 'Holy cow', 'Dangit', 'rip', 'bleh', 'Bro', 'ngl'), or spaced-out text. Do not judge whether the tone is appropriate; score only how much such language appears.
proposals.rationale: A chatty register can bias a reader toward or away from a post independently of the solution method. R31 opens with 'Bro,' and laments 'rip'; R02 exclaims 'Holy cow this configuration is so nice'; R58 uses spaced-out 's t o r a g e'.
proposals.upstream_parent: poster's audience (chatting with peers vs writing for a permanent record)

proposals.name: Rich forum markup and structured formatting
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post employs advanced forum markup: color tags, bold/italic section headers, bullet lists, hide/spoiler blocks, custom LaTeX macros, or boxed answers. Do not judge whether the formatting is helpful; score only how much advanced markup is present.
proposals.rationale: Practised forum users often deploy rich markup, which may impress a rubric regardless of whether the underlying method is canonical. R02 uses a bold 'Walk-Through' header and bullet points; R53 uses colored section headers and a boxed conclusion; R55 uses color-coded claims.
proposals.upstream_parent: typographic habit / poster's practice in the format

proposals.name: Validation-seeking and uncertain posture
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post is framed as a question, request for checking, or expression of doubt rather than a confident solution. Look for phrases like 'Does this work?', 'Can someone please explain why', 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?', or 'I'm getting X, is this right?'. Do not judge whether the uncertainty is warranted; score only how much the text seeks validation.
proposals.rationale: A post can contain substantial mathematics yet be framed as an inquiry, which may inflate a checklist score without matching the canonical approach. R18 asks 'Does this work?'; R37 asks 'Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?'; R38 asks 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?'
proposals.upstream_parent: poster's confidence / audience (asking peers)

proposals.name: Extraneous generalization or added content
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post includes content that goes well beyond solving the stated problem, such as generalized theorems, unrelated observations, extended theory, or alternative method sketches appended after the main solution. Do not judge whether the extra content is interesting; score only how much extraneous or extended material is present.
proposals.rationale: Overly general or bonus content can make a post appear more thorough without reflecting the canonical approach. R02 ends with 'Other Observations' and an 'Added Later' note; R42 develops a full theory of random walks on n-gons; R33 tacks on '(Instead of angle chasing, inversion would also work.)'
proposals.upstream_parent: process dynamics / motivation (exploration rather than answering)

proposals.name: Explicit self-assessment labels
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post labels its own solution with qualitative descriptors such as 'cheap', 'fast', 'overkill', 'scuffed', 'troll', 'cursed', 'different', 'alternative', or 'simple'. Do not judge whether the label is accurate; score only how many such self-assessment phrases appear.
proposals.rationale: Self-labeling can bias a scorer independently of the actual mathematical approach. R09 calls itself 'very cheap but fast'; R40 says 'Scuffed troll solution'; R54 says 'cursed solution which somehow got a 7/7'; R04 calls itself 'a different solution'.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing / self-consciousness about the method

proposals.name: Collaborative attribution to other users
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post explicitly credits or mentions other forum users as collaborators or co-solvers (e.g., 'Solved with [user]', 'thanks to [user]'). Do not judge whether collaboration is good; score only how much attribution to others appears.
proposals.rationale: Mentioning co-solvers is a social marker unrelated to whether the method matches the canonical write-up. R15 says 'Solved with [b]mathapple101[/b]'; R34 lists 'Solved with [b]S.Ragnork1729[/b], [b]SilverBlaze_SY[/b] and [b]HACK_IN_MATHS[/b]'.
proposals.upstream_parent: social effects / collaborative process

proposals.name: Extreme brevity and step compression
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the solution is terse, skipping intermediate steps or using phrases like 'clearly', 'obviously', 'easy to see', 'trivial', or providing a very short argument without derivation. Do not judge whether brevity is good or bad; score only how much the text compresses or omits steps.
proposals.rationale: An expert may write very briefly yet still match the canonical approach; brevity can bias a rubric that rewards completeness. R10 gives a one-sentence counterexample; R05 gives a two-line argument; R46 provides a short calculation with '@above thanks!' and little exposition.
proposals.upstream_parent: poster's standing / willingness to compress routine steps

proposals.name: Contest-recollection and temporal language
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post uses language that dates it to the contest period or indicates later editing, such as 'during the contest', 'my solution during the contest', 'added later', 'edit:', or reflections on the testing experience. Do not judge whether temporal language is appropriate; score only how much such language appears.
proposals.rationale: Posts written from contest memory or edited later carry temporal fingerprints that do not determine the solution method. R16 says 'My solution during the contest'; R02 includes an '[i]Added Later:[/i]' note; R35 discusses what 'I did' and worries about points.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing

proposals.name: Display math prevalence
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the post uses display math environments (e.g., \[...\], $$...$$, align, eqnarray) rather than inline math. A high score means most equations are displayed prominently; a low score means most math is inline. Do not judge whether display math is better; score only the ratio.
proposals.rationale: Reliance on display math is a formatting style of practised users and may correlate with canonical write-up style without being about the approach itself. R42 uses heavy display math and eqnarray; R10 uses only inline math; R59 uses a single prominent display equation.
proposals.upstream_parent: typographic habit / poster's practice in the format

proposals.name: Named theorem as proof engine
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the post explicitly names a widely-recognized theorem (e.g., Cauchy-Schwarz, Radical Axis, Pigeonhole Principle, Miquel's Theorem) AND that theorem is the primary deductive tool driving the solution forward. Score 0 if no theorem is named, or a theorem is name-dropped without being applied.
proposals.rationale: In dense_high_card_low items R01 ('Radical Axis on (BCXDF),...') and R43 ('equality case of Cauchy-Schwarz'), the named theorem IS the engine of the proof, signaling the canonical approach. In dense_low_card_high items like R05 and R08, no named theorem appears at all, yet the scorecard still rates them highly—over-crediting computational correctness over technique alignment.

proposals.name: Claim decomposition with individual proofs
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the argument is decomposed into multiple separately labeled claims (e.g., 'Claim 1,' 'Claim 2'), each accompanied by its own proof or justification. Score 0 if the argument is a single monolithic block or has no identifiable intermediate assertions.
proposals.rationale: R01 builds six labeled claims each with a proof, and R54 uses four labeled claims—both dense-high. R05 and R25 have no claim structure at all yet scorecard rates them high. The claim-proof structure is a hallmark of how official write-ups organize geometry and FE solutions, and the dense model appears to key on it.

proposals.name: Systematic equation evaluation protocol
proposals.instruction: For functional equations or identity problems, score 10 if the post systematically evaluates the given assertion at multiple standard input pairs (e.g., P(0,0), P(x,0), P(0,y), P(x,x²)) in an organized sequence. Score 0 if evaluations are ad hoc, unorganized, or absent. For non-equation problems, score based on whether the post establishes a standard initial framework systematically.
proposals.rationale: R04, R11, R22, R32, R51, R54, R56, R58 all follow the P(x,y) → P(0,0) → P(x,0) → P(x,x²) protocol—eight dense-high FE solutions. R13 and R16 (dense_low_card_high) use non-standard substitutions (defining g(x) = f(x+1)) that deviate from this protocol, which the scorecard fails to penalize.

proposals.name: Central structural observation explicitness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the post explicitly states the key mathematical identity, similarity, or structural observation that unlocks the problem (e.g., 'Note that F_{2n}/F_n = F_{n+1}+F_{n-1}' or 'triangle AII_1 is similar to AI_2X'). The observation should be prominent, not buried. Score 0 if the key insight is implicit, never stated, or obscured.
proposals.rationale: R40 explicitly states the Fibonacci identity, and R41 explicitly states the similar-triangle observation—both dense-high despite being informal posts. R19 applies Minkowski's inequality without ever stating the geometric interpretation (sum of distances) that constitutes the central insight, which may explain its low dense score despite high card score.

proposals.name: Absence of unconventional-approach markers
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the post contains NO language self-labeling the approach as unusual, unconventional, or excessive (e.g., 'troll,' 'scuffed,' 'overkill,' 'different,' 'cheap,' 'ridiculous'). Score 0 if multiple such markers appear, signaling the author themselves recognizes the approach deviates from standard.
proposals.rationale: R05 ('Scuffed troll solution'), R28 ('ridiculous and yet ultimately equivalent...overkill'), R10 ('different from the others'), R25 ('very cheap but fast'), and R30 ('for those who understand less') all self-label as non-standard and are dense_low. Dense-high items like R01, R43, R34 contain no such markers. The author's own awareness of non-canonical approach is a strong signal the dense model detects.

proposals.name: Argument self-containment without external reference
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the post contains a complete self-contained argument that does not reference other posts, wiki solutions, or ask questions about its own validity. Score 0 if the post references external content, asks 'does this work?', or depends on prior posts for its argument.
proposals.rationale: R39 references and questions a wiki solution, R45 asks 'Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?', and R46 says 'I already addressed this in my previous post'—all dense_low_card_high. R01 and R22 are fully self-contained—dense_high. The dense model may interpret external dependence as evidence the approach is not the self-sufficient canonical one.

proposals.name: Candidate solution verification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the post explicitly verifies that all proposed solutions/candidates actually satisfy the original problem conditions (e.g., 'All three clearly work,' or direct substitution back). Score 0 if candidates are proposed without any verification.
proposals.rationale: R22 ('All three clearly work'), R54 ('It is easy to check that these work'), and R56 include explicit verification—dense-high. R13 and R16 (dense_low) state the solutions but do not include a verification step. The canonical write-up conventionally includes a check, and the dense model appears to credit this.

proposals.name: Global consistency argument for classifications
proposals.instruction: For problems asking to 'find all' functions/structures: score 10 if the post explicitly addresses whether the solution could vary pointwise (i.e., argues that the same answer holds globally, not just at individual points). Score 0 if this issue is never mentioned. For non-classification problems, score 10 if the argument addresses all relevant global/local distinctions.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('Note that we need not check for pointwise trap as the value of k cannot alternate'), R22 (handles the trap in detail), and R56 ('the value of f(c)/c² is fixed and cannot alternate') all explicitly address this—dense-high. R13 and R16 (dense_low_card_high) never mention the pointwise trap, a critical component of the canonical FE approach.

proposals.name: Construction motivation from constraints
proposals.instruction: For construction or existence problems, score 10 if the construction is derived from the problem's constraints (e.g., solving a system of equations to find what the construction must satisfy). Score 0 if the construction is stated without explanation of where it came from.
proposals.rationale: R34 derives the triplet by setting up pairwise-sum equations and solving—dense-high. R31 states a=2x²-4x, b=2x²+1, c=2x²+4x with minimal motivation. R26 uses a greedy algorithm description. The dense model credits the constraint-derived construction as matching the canonical approach.

proposals.name: Algebraic step transparency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if all key algebraic manipulations are shown step by step with no major leaps. Score 0 if the post jumps directly to results with significant intermediate algebra omitted.
proposals.rationale: R03 shows detailed algebraic manipulation throughout its case analysis—dense-high. R19 condenses the entire Minkowski argument into one line with the factorization (S_n-n²)(S_n+n²)=1·289 appearing without derivation—dense_low. The scorecard credits the elegant one-liner; the dense model may see the omitted steps as a departure from the canonical derivation.

proposals.name: Presentation definitiveness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the solution is presented as definitive and correct without hedging, doubt, or appeals for validation. Score 0 if the post expresses uncertainty, asks if the approach is valid, or indicates the solver gave up.
proposals.rationale: R12 ('I'm hoping its not more than 1 point off'), R35 ('didn't really know why... I stopped'), R53 ('I sure do hope it is valid'), and R40 ('didn't have courage so i was scared') all express doubt—these are mixed but tend toward dense_high when the underlying approach is canonical despite the doubt. However, R45 explicitly asks 'why 391 is incorrect' showing the answer is wrong—dense_low. Definitive presentation (R01, R43) correlates with canonical write-up style.

proposals.name: Case structure completeness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the post explicitly identifies and handles all necessary cases with clear case boundaries (e.g., 'Case 1: q=2,' 'Case 2: q>2'), and the case decomposition covers the entire problem. Score 0 if cases are missing, incomplete, or not clearly delineated.
proposals.rationale: R03 exhausts Cases 1-3 with subcases 3a-3d—dense-high. R50 uses a clean Case 1/Case 2 structure. R38 presents a complex algebraic claim but the case structure is less standard. The dense model appears to credit systematic case decomposition matching the canonical proof organization.

proposals.name: Notational conventionality and consistency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the post uses standard, conventional mathematical notation throughout (e.g., P(x,y) for assertions, standard function/variable names, conventional geometric notation). Score 0 if notation is highly non-standard, inconsistent, or introduces unusual symbols/conventions.
proposals.rationale: R28 introduces computation in F_25 with non-standard conventions ('without loss of generality assume that i = 2')—dense_low_card_high. R01, R22, R43 all use standard notation—dense-high. The scorecard credits R28's correctness; the dense model may read the unconventional notation as a departure from canonical approach.

proposals.name: Progressive argument flow from setup to conclusion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the argument follows a clear progressive structure: initial setup → key intermediate results → main argument → conclusion, with each section building on the previous. Score 0 if the argument is disorganized, circular, or has sections that don't connect logically.
proposals.rationale: R34 follows a textbook progression (Strategy → Construction → Bounds → Covering → Conclusion) with labeled sections—dense-high. R53 describes an approach in fragmented, disorganized prose ('I did something like induction... somewhere in there I threw in ceiling/floor functions')—lower dense score despite potentially valid approach. R01 builds six claims in logical sequence toward radical axes.

proposals.name: Method sophistication proportionality to problem
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the mathematical tools used are proportionate in sophistication to the apparent difficulty of the problem (e.g., elementary number theory for a modular arithmetic problem). Score 0 if the method is wildly over-powered (e.g., finite field theory for a root-of-unity computation) or under-powered for the problem.
proposals.rationale: R28 uses F_25 finite field computation for a problem solvable by identifying an 8th root of unity—dense_low_card_high. R06 constructs elaborate perpendicular line verifications for a simple angle formula—dense_low. R43 uses Cauchy-Schwarz for an inequality where it is the natural tool—dense-high. The dense model appears to credit methods that match the problem's intended difficulty level.

proposals.name: Colloquial and emotional register
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text uses informal colloquial language, slang, self-deprecation, emoticons, or emotional interjections (e.g., 'rip', 'cuz', ':(', 'nooooo', 'Bro'), as opposed to standard mathematical prose. 0 = entirely formal; 10 = heavily colloquial/emotional. Do not judge whether informality is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('I assumed... didn't really know why... :(') and R22 ('Bro... cuz im dumb... RIP') are dense_high_card_low: the dense model may key on approach content while the scorecard is put off by register. R09 ('Dangit') and R25 ('Holy cow') show the same split.
proposals.upstream_parent: poster's practice in the format / audience expectation

proposals.name: Structured claim-proof formatting
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text uses structured formatting elements typical of olympiad-style write-ups: labeled Claims, color-coded or bold headers, italicized 'Proof.' markers, or section dividers (e.g., horizontal rules). 0 = plain prose with no structural markers; 10 = extensive use of such elements throughout. Do not judge whether such formatting improves the solution.
proposals.rationale: R13, R32, R35, R36, and R51 all deploy colored bold claim headers and are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model responds to content while the scorecard may discount or the reverse. R19 and R24 (dense_low_card_high) also use heavy formatting, showing the feature cuts both ways and is predictive of disagreement.
proposals.upstream_parent: poster's familiarity with forum markup conventions

proposals.name: Explicit references to other posts or solutions
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text explicitly references, quotes, or responds to other posts, solutions, wiki write-ups, or specific users in the thread (e.g., '@above', 'the wiki solution', 'similar to above', 'different from the others', 'my previous post'). 0 = entirely self-contained; 10 = heavily dependent on prior content. Do not judge whether references are appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('I am confused on the wiki solution #2'), R06 ('@above'), and R10 ('@above thanks!') are dense_high_card_low; R31 ('A different solution for those who understand less about complex numbers') and R57 ('Um no, I already addressed this in my previous post') are dense_low_card_high. Referencing prior content signals thread position, not approach novelty.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream

proposals.name: Contest-process and scoring meta-narrative
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text contains meta-commentary about the contest or problem-solving experience: time spent, difficulty comparisons to other problems, expected or received scores, or solving conditions. 0 = no such meta-commentary; 10 = extensive meta-narrative. Do not judge whether such commentary is useful.
proposals.rationale: R07 ('It took ~1.3 hours... #4 was far harder!') and R37 ('I'm hoping its not more than 1 point off') are dense_high_card_low. R02 ('My solution during the contest (different from the others)') and R39 ('my cursed solution which somehow got a 7/7') show the same pattern. Contest-experienced posters may produce both meta-narrative and approach-matching solutions.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing / contest experience

proposals.name: Collaboration credits by username
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text explicitly credits or acknowledges other forum users by username for collaboration, discussion, or assistance. 0 = no credits at all; 10 = extensive acknowledgment of multiple users. Do not judge whether crediting others is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R29 ('Solved with S.Ragnork1729, SilverBlaze_SY and HACK_IN_MATHS') is dense_high_card_low, while R55 ('Solved with mathapple101') is dense_low_card_high. The presence of usernames is a social-dynamics fingerprint unrelated to whether the mathematical approach matches a canonical write-up.
proposals.upstream_parent: social dynamics / collaboration patterns

proposals.name: Hide and spoiler block deployment
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the solution text is wrapped in hide or spoiler blocks ([hide=...] tags). 0 = no hide blocks at all; 10 = the entire solution enclosed in hide blocks. Do not judge whether hiding solutions is good practice.
proposals.rationale: R03 ('[hide=sketch]'), R18 ('[hide=solution]'), R26 ('[hide="Solution"]') are dense_high_card_low; R02 ('[hide="My solution during the contest..."]') and R54 ('[hide = very cheap but fast solution]') are dense_low_card_high. The choice to hide is a convention/audience signal, not an approach-match signal.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience awareness / forum convention practice

proposals.name: Mathematical machinery beyond problem level
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text employs mathematical theorems, techniques, or frameworks that appear substantially more advanced or elaborate than the problem's apparent difficulty level would call for. Judge the problem's level from the problem statement only. 0 = techniques well-matched to the problem; 10 = extreme overkill. Do not judge whether the advanced techniques are valid or correct.
proposals.rationale: R05 uses roots-of-unity filters and Fourier analysis on cyclic groups for an AMC probability problem (dense_high_card_low). R33 deploys finite field arithmetic for a multiple-choice computation (dense_low_card_high). R49 cites the hook-length formula for a counting problem. Advanced training may correlate with both machinery display and canonical approach selection.

proposals.name: Uncertainty hedging and validation-seeking
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text expresses uncertainty about its own correctness, asks readers for validation, or poses rhetorical questions about its own work (e.g., 'Does this work?', 'Wouldn't that be overcounting?', 'Can someone please explain why...?', 'I sure do hope it is valid'). 0 = fully confident presentation; 10 = pervasive uncertainty throughout. Do not judge whether the uncertainty is justified.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('Wouldn't that be overcounting?') and R27 ('Can someone please explain why 391 is incorrect?') are dense_low_card_high, while R08 ('Does this work?') is also dense_low_card_high. R07 ('I sure do hope it is valid') is dense_high_card_low. Validation-seeking is a confidence/experience fingerprint, not an approach-match indicator.
proposals.upstream_parent: poster confidence / experience level

proposals.name: Solution verbosity and structural elaborateness
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT of the solution's verbosity, as measured by word count, number of labeled claims/lemmas/cases/subcases, depth of structural nesting, and overall argument length. 0 = extremely terse (a few lines); 10 = extremely elaborate (many sections, deep case analysis, hundreds of words). Do not judge whether verbosity is good or bad.
proposals.rationale: R19 and R24 are extremely long and elaborately structured (dense_low_card_high), while R01 and R14 are very terse (dense_high_card_low). Conversely R39 and R40 are long (dense_high_card_low). Verbosity predicts disagreement because the scorecard may reward elaborateness while the dense model keys on approach content regardless of length.
proposals.upstream_parent: writing style / thoroughness practice

proposals.name: Verbalized solving-process narrative
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the EXTENT to which the text narrates the problem-solving thought process — describing what the solver tried, assumed, doubted, or realized mid-solution (e.g., 'I assumed the triangles were...', 'halfway through the algebra', 'I didn't realize it was actually doable') — as opposed to presenting only the finished mathematical argument. 0 = purely presentational; 10 = extensive process narrative. Do not judge whether such narrative is helpful.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('I assumed... started bashing... started doubting myself and I stopped') and R07 ('I did something like induction... eventually went up to the next case... somewhere in there I threw in ceiling/floor functions') are dense_high_card_low, suggesting the dense model keys on approach while process-narrative distracts the scorecard. R22 ('i didn't have courage... was scared to bash... didn't realize') shows the same split.
